utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. There's one matter to raise today before we start business today. The Chamber would like to deal with the matter of the time for cross-examination of John Wilson before he begins his testimony. Mr. Karadzic, we noted that at the beginning of the Prosecution case that we did not consider your estimate for the time you need to cross-examine the upcoming Prosecution witnesses to be reasonable and that the Chamber may have to consider imposing time constraints on your cross-examination. Since then, we have given you considerable latitude in taking the time you wanted for cross-examination. In so doing, we acknowledge that you have not had previous experience in conducting cross-examination and that latitude was required. The Chamber has also given you advice on how to approach your cross-examination, such as how to formulate your questions to witnesses, to stop making comments, and to stop reading lengthy passages of documents to witnesses, and it has, on multiple occasions, encouraged you to move to more relevant lines of questioning and focus on the charges against you. As a result of finding that your estimate for the last witness, Mr. Richard Philipps, was unreasonable, the Chamber decided it was necessary to limit you to five hours, which proved to be certainly sufficient time. In light of the experience to date, the Chamber has determined that it is now both necessary and justified to establish the time available for your cross-examination of each witness. However, the Chamber emphasises that this is for reasons of trial management and is not to be regarded as a sanction. In establishing the time available to you, we note that this is a common practice in cases before the Tribunal and that the approach most regularly applied is that of numerical equivalence between the parties. However, in light of your status as a self-represented accused, and the predominance of Rule 92 ter witnesses in the Prosecution's case, we will instead be making our assessment based on a consideration of a number of factors. First and foremost, we will take into consideration your estimate of the time you needed for the witness. The other factors we will look at are: Prosecution's estimation of time for examination-in-chief, scope of anticipated testimony, type of witness, which will in most instances be Rule 92 ter, quantity and type of written evidence proffered for the witness, number of associated exhibits tendered for witnesses, and length of testimony and cross-examination in previous cases. The Chamber will endeavour to inform you of the time you will have for cross-examination sufficiently in advance of the witness appearing before the Tribunal, which will generally be several days in advance. In setting time constraints, we remain amenable to giving you additional time on a case-by-case basis if you make a reasonable request for more time and the Chamber is satisfied that your cross-examination has been generally effective and the evidence being elicited by you is relevant to the case against you. That said, following a consideration of the above-mentioned factors, we've determined that you will have seven hours for cross-examination of Mr. John Wilson. That said, for the scheduling matter, we will sit today, tomorrow, and the day after three 90-minute sessions, i.e., 9.00 to 10.30, 11.00 to 12.30, and 1.30 to 3.00. We can bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Before we do that, I actually have an oral motion I would like to make concerning a Rule 68 violation, and this will be, I guess, our third motion for disclosure violation. And it pertains to materials we just received with respect to this witness, John Wilson. It might be easier if I can provide to you, either by e-mail or through some other means, the two documents that are in question, but on the 17th of June we received two documents from the Prosecution which they said were potentially Rule 68 material, but which had been withheld from disclosure pursuant to Rule 70, and those two documents, in my view, do constitute Rule 68 material. One document which -- they're both authored by the witness. One of them is a memorandum in which he states that Mladic does not always follow political directions. And in the other document, which is an assessment of the different armies' intentions at a certain point in time, he states that the Muslim side may find it necessary to mount an offensive to obtain foreign intervention. And those are two issues that we think are live issues in the case and that these documents should have been disclosed to us at a more timely -- certainly, as soon as practicable, which is not on the eve of the witness's testimony. Dr. Karadzic has not had a chance to look at these documents yet because of late disclosure, and so we would be asking as a remedy that he be given additional time before beginning his cross-examination to deal with the late disclosure of these materials. So that's my submission at this time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I ask you, for clarification, what do you mean by "being given additional time for cross-examination"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: To commence his cross-examination -- we would like some time, after the Prosecutor's direct examination has been completed, before Dr. Karadzic has to commence his cross-examination, in order for him to be able to review and assimilate these documents, if necessary, into his cross-examination outline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would he have difficulty in starting his cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Perhaps he's better equipped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll consider the matter in due course. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say a few words?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, with respect to these documents, there are a number of documents which the Prosecution is interested in, and I was disclosed many documents last week which I'm interested in, so I didn't have the time to look through them all. Now, as far as your instructions and guide-lines go, I highly appreciate all the suggestions and proposals you make, but my problem with the witnesses is that I have a problem with these witnesses that are bias and expand their story. They answer my question, but then add a "but" and continue, so I have to challenge those additional things that they state. So I'd like to ask the Trial Chamber to protect me in that sense. When I'm asking for an answer, I don't want the witness to behave as a Prosecutor. And there are witnesses that have even misled the Prosecution, saying that they have a case against me. Donia did that, too. He was fighting tooth and nail to portray the Prosecution in a good light, so then I have to introduce new documents when the need arises during the cross-examination and testimony of witnesses of that type. So if I can count on your protection, when I say "thank you," that suffices, to protect the witness from expanding. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I appreciate your concerns. All accused would have the same concerns. But rest assured that one of the tasks of the Trial Chamber, consisting of experienced Judges, is to filter out any obvious bias or prejudice. It's part of the fair trial process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Finally, bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, General. If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please make yourself comfortable. Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good morning. Please state your full name. Good morning. Please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I am John Brian Wilson.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you're a retired brigadier general in the Australian Armed Forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You testified previously in the Krajisnik case on the 17th and 18th of May, 2005, and in the Perisic case on the 3rd of November, 2008; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Subsequent to that testimony, a statement was taken from you which amalgamated evidence from your previous testimony and statements, with some additional observations as well as references to certain documents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With Your Honours' leave, I'll proceed with the requirements of Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: On the 26th of March, 2009, you signed an amalgamated witness statement, making handwritten corrections to paragraphs 49 and 81. And if I could ask for 65 ter 22293 to be brought up on the screen, please, Mr. Registrar. Is that your signature at the bottom of page 1?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And could you please go to page 2?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that your initial at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And did you initial each page?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you go to page 37, the last page, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that's your signature there under the witness acknowledgment?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to review the statement that you signed on the 26th of March, 2009, and the exhibits referred to therein?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Are there two corrections you wish to make?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, there are.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is the first one a typographical error? If we could go to page 18 of the statement, please. Concerning the date in the first sentence of paragraph 76, the "29th of May, 1995," should read "29th of May, 1992"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 23 of the document, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The second correction you wish to make was in relation to paragraph 91. The first sentence, the words "the same day" should read "the next day"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With these corrections, do you confirm that your amalgamated statement accurately reflects your evidence and that you would provide the same answers to questions if you were asked, under oath, about these topics today?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I seek to have the amalgamated witness statement 65 ter 22293 admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P1029.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With Your Honour's leave, I'll now read a brief summary of the witness's evidence. The witness, General John Wilson, is a retired career military officer from the Australian armed forces, with 34 years of service. During his career, he held numerous command positions in the Australian Army. He was deployed to Vietnam and Malaysia. He participated in United Nations missions in Lebanon and Jerusalem. General Wilson was seconded to the UN to serve in the former Yugoslavia during 1992 and 1993 in a number of posts. In January and February 1992, as the senior military liaison officer to the United Nations Military Liaison Mission to the former Yugoslavia, he was involved in negotiations regarding the deployment of UNPROFOR to the former Yugoslavia. From March 1992, he was the chief of the United Nations Military Observers, a subordinate part of the UNPROFOR mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In that capacity, he was involved in various high-level negotiations with political and military representatives of the warring factions, including negotiations to evacuate JNA barracks in Sarajevo, negotiations to open the airport in Sarajevo, negotiations to evacuate the JNA from Dubrovnik, and negotiations to implement the no-fly zone over Bosnia. In December 1992, General Wilson became the military adviser to Cyrus Vance, Lord Owen, and the late ambassador -- and then later Ambassador Stoltenberg at the international Conference for the former Yugoslavia, where he also served as the UNPROFOR liaison officer to the conference. He remained in those positions until December 1993. General Wilson's written evidence describes the deployment of the United Nations Military Observers in Bosnia and the work they and he performed, observations relating to the shelling and sniping of civilians in Sarajevo by Bosnian Serb forces, descriptions of reports he received about ethnic cleansing in Eastern Bosnia, descriptions of negotiations in which he participated, and interactions he had with representatives of the various parties engaged in the conflict, including the accused Radovan Karadzic, General Ratko Mladic, Biljana Plavsic, Slobodan Milosevic, and General Zivota Panic. He will discuss some of these aspects in his oral testimony today. General Wilson's written evidence describes complaints that Lord Owen made directly to Bosnian Serb representatives during peace negotiations about ethnic cleansing and military observations directed against the civilian population. General Wilson recalls that Dr. Karadzic's reaction was generally a restatement of the need to defend the Serb people and the need for a Serb republic. That concludes the brief summary of the witness's evidence. Your Honour, before I proceed with examination, I seek leave to add an exhibit to the Prosecution's 65 ter exhibit list. It's 65 ter 22854. This document is a protest letter dated the 2nd of June, 1992, from Sefer Halilovic, addressed to UNPROFOR, for the attention of Colonel Wilson, as he then was. This document is relevant to notice and crimes alleged in the Prijedor municipality. The document was identified during a review of an additional ISU search relating to the witness. It was disclosed to the accused as soon as it came to our attention. It was disclosed on the 15th of June, 2010.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it one of the items subject to the 18th of June filing?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's listed as an additional exhibit, the third-to-last -- the third-to-last exhibit on the 92 ter notification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We're going to object to that. We're having a lot of problems with late disclosure with respect to this witness and an absence of showing why this couldn't have been disclosed to us earlier. We object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, the Chamber is not satisfied why this document could not have been disclosed to the accused earlier, and, as such, we are not giving leave to this document to be added to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: General Wilson, you were chief of the United Nations Military Observers from the 8th of March, 1992, until the 15th of November, 1992. Can you briefly explain for the Trial Chamber the UNMO's -- United Nations Military Observers' mandate in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: There were approximately 75 military observers when UNPROFOR was first established. Their mission was to deploy to two areas within Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they were the Bihac area and the Mostar area. And the reason for that was, under the Vance Plan, which is the basis for UNPROFOR's deployment, there was some concern that there was growing ethnic tension in those areas and there was a need to monitor what was happening there; hence, the deployment of the military observers. Now -- I'm sorry, if I can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It's important to realise at this stage that UNPROFOR, when it deployed in March 1992, had no operational role and focus in Bosnia whatsoever. It was deploying because of the conflict in Croatia, and it's only with the outbreak of hostilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina that a mandate emerged for UNPROFOR, and that became then the focus, really, of most of UNPROFOR's operations for the next year or so or two years that I was there. The military observers, as part of UNPROFOR, received a number of mandate enhancements during 1992, and eventually there were some 350 to 400 military observers as part of my group deployed mainly throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, but still approximately 60 in the UNPAs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you describe briefly their duties and responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: There were two types of military observers. Some were under the direct command of sector commanders and some were under my direct command. That defined their reporting channels. But, in essence, they were there to facilitate communication between the parties, to acquire information and report that back to the UN, and to lend their good officers to perform any tasks that might assist the parties in resolving the conflict; for example, exchanges of bodies or escorting and arranging of humanitarian relief.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At paragraph 56 of your statement -- maybe, Your Honour, can the witness have a copy of his statement in front of him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P1029.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You describe there your personal observations of shelling and sniping within the city of Sarajevo as heavy, intense, and widespread. How did you have an opportunity to observe this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I was actually living outside of the PTT building initially, living in two apartments, so I was able to observe, I guess, a domestic existence within UNPROFOR, certainly for the first month that I was down there. In addition to that, I was residing later in the PTT and working from there, and it was a building which afforded a broad observation of that area of Sarajevo, so you were able to see and hear a great deal of what was happening in that part of Sarajevo. I have to say that in March, April, and May of 1992, Sarajevo was not a place that you wandered around idly out of tourist interest. It was a very dangerous place, and one only travelled when it was absolutely necessary. So the majority of my observations were confined to the city centre and to the area around the PTT, Dobrinja, Nedarici, and perhaps the airport.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And can you give a brief description of what you observed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, for the whole period I was there from the 22nd of March to the 24th of June, with one short 10-day break, I observed that the city was subjected to almost constant artillery fire. There was widespread sniping. There was fighting going on in selected areas of the city, heavy fighting. But I would say that a lot of the military activity was -- a lot of the artillery fire and mortar fire was randomly distributed around the city, and there were very few areas which escaped at least some damage from this activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'd like to focus your attention on the latter part of paragraph 56 of your statement, where it reads: "On most days, for the six weeks I was in Sarajevo, artillery fire was very heavy and directed virtually at the whole city, so it was widespread. The attacks were intense. On some days, it would last 16 hours." Are you able to comment on which force was involved in the artillery fired that was directed at the whole city?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I am able to comment, and the answer is that the fire was directed and produced almost exclusively by the Serb forces who were investing the city. Presidency forces had very little in the way of heavy armaments, so any artillery or mortar fire coming into the city was virtually all initiated by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Turning to paragraph -

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. What do you mean by "Presidency forces"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm referring to the combined forces of the Muslim and Croat forces who were residing within the city and who were attempting to defend the city, and who were commanded by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, led by President Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Though I must say there were also significant members of Serb fighters fighting within that organisation also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Turning to paragraph 57 of your statement, you say that: "I have been involved in conventional military operations as a soldier, and I have never seen such weight of fire used, and particularly not against civilian targets." Can you describe your points of comparison?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, as a young officer, I deployed to Vietnam for 12 months and fought there as an infantry officer. Certainly, in comparison there and also in my later experience in Southern Lebanon, when that area was occupied by Israeli forces, what I was able to observe in Beirut, once again when I was with the UN, none of those experiences came close to the intensity of the fighting that took place in Sarajevo in the six weeks or so that I was there in early 1992. I have to say that the way that artillery, mortars, and other heavy weapons were directed into the city impressed me as being random, widespread, and inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: To be clear, what forces were engaged in the weight of fire that you've referred to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Sutherland. Before you go on, can I read that sentence again? You read 57, para 57, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If I read it again: "I have been involved in conventional military operations as a soldier, and I had never seen such weight of fire used, and particularly not against civilian targets." Does that read well, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's how it reads, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So, General, to be clear, what forces were engaged in the weight of fire that you refer to in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: The overwhelming weight of fire was produced by the Serb forces investing the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned in paragraph 83 of the statement that you recalled the period between 14 May and late June as being one of constant daily heavy bombardments, with only brief respites. Do you recall any times where the Serb forces attacked -- where the Serb forces' attacks on Sarajevo were particularly heavy?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I remember the period from the 14th of May, three or four days, in which there was heavy fighting in the vicinity of the PTT, Dobrinja, Ilidza, that area that I was able to observe more closely, but also I was generally aware of the noise of battle taking place in other parts of the city. And then in the period of late May, there was very heavy fighting taking place in the area of Grubaca [phoen], I think it's pronounced. It's in the vicinity of the "Marsal Tito" Barracks. And that lasted, really, until early June. And then there was a third series of heavy fighting which was initiated or commenced immediately after the airport agreement was signed or the day after the airport agreement was signed, and that continued from the 6th of June until I left the city on the 24th of June, with very little respite. The fighting was almost continuous from the 14th of May until the 24th of June. There was the odd day of respite. And on some occasions, there was absolute adherence to a cease-fire so that something of mutual interest to the parties could take place. For example, the evacuation of the Tito Barracks, the JNA forces there, was affected under absolute quiet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: General, if we could just go to the sentence that we referred to in paragraph 57 that His Honour Judge Kwon drew your attention to. It's perhaps the double negative. Was the weight of fire used against civilian targets?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: The weight of fire in Sarajevo against civilian targets was at a scale that I'd not experienced anywhere else in my operational experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where was the Bosnian Serb military barracks located?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: There were a number, Counsel. I'm not sure which one you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where did you have your meetings with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: All my meetings with General Mladic were at the Lukavica JNA barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was your travel in and around Sarajevo restricted in any way?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: We were only -- from the 14th of May until the 24th of June, we were only able to sensibly travel around the city in armoured vehicles. And then on approximately 70 to 80 per cent of occasions, we would draw fire from one or other of the parties. It would not be fair to accuse any one party of attacking the UN. It was our belief that all parties were actively engaged in the activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did you do about the firing on the UN vehicles?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: We had -- or I had arranged, very early in my stay there, after the 14th of May, arranged for each of the parties to have a liaison officer reside in our headquarters in the PTT to facilitate communications, and we were able to use these liaison officers to protest these attacks against UN forces. Also, after one particularly heavy attack, I suspended UN operations for 24 hours and informed the parties unless they could guarantee the safety of my forces, we would not be resuming operations to assist them in their concerns. I also reported formally these attacks to my superior officer, General Nambiar, who was then located in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can I please have 65 ter 31753 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: General, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It's a intercept communication between Colonel Cadjo, who was the JNA liaison officer located in the PTT, and he's talking to General Mladic about me travelling from the PTT to Lukavica for a meeting with Mrs. Plavsic, and he's asking for safe -- my safe passage in the armoured vehicles I was travelling in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And does he give --

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: He gives them assurance that we would be allowed to proceed safely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, pursuant to earlier rulings in relation to intercepts, I'd ask that this be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI P1030, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you know personally Colonel Cadjo at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honour. He spent perhaps a week or so residing in the PTT with us, and he was actively participating in the negotiations for the withdrawal of the JNA from the barracks in Sarajevo. He also acted as an interpreter for the UN, between the UN and the JNA. I think he may have had previous UN experience himself. He was quite a professional officer and tried to do the best he could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was his name Cadjo or Cadjo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: C-a-d-j-o or something like that. I'm not sure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can return to your statement at paragraph 73, you describe a meeting between General Mladic and Mrs. Plavsic on the -- I'm sorry. Before we leave this intercept, the date of the intercept in the B/C/S version is the 25th of May, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's what it says on the Bosnian Serb translation or statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. So in paragraph 73, you describe a meeting that you had with General Mladic and Mrs. Plavsic on the 25th of May, 1992, where General Mladic made a threat that if JNA personnel from Sarajevo barracks were not evacuated within three days, General Mladic would engage the city with heavy artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, that was the substance of the meeting, and I reported that to my superiors in Belgrade. I also passed that information on to the Presidency, through their liaison officer in the PTT.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall what Mrs. Plavsic's response was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: She supported that position. She certainly didn't contradict anything that General Mladic said. She was also anxious to see -- the problem of the JNA being evacuated from the Sarajevo barracks, she wanted to see it resolved as quickly as possible too. It seemed to me that with the chief Serb military officer and a member of the Presidency passing that information formally to me and asking me to relay that to other parties, that it was a formal position of the Serb political leadership.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I can just correct myself, I referred to paragraph 73. In fact, it's paragraph 72 and 73 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 76, you refer to shelling by Serb territorial forces on the night of the 28th of May, 1992. Do you recall the shelling? And if so, can you please describe its intensity?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: The shelling took place in the evening of the 28th of May, from approximately at 5.00 in the evening until about 1.00 the next morning. It was particularly heavy even by Sarajevo standards. It was widespread. It did not appear to be related to any conflict on the front-line. It was in-depth and scattered around the city, although there appeared to be particular emphasis on directing fire into the city centre. But even around the PTT building there was a lot of artillery fire, mortar fire, during that evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And at the time of the shelling on the 28th, had the barracks been evacuated?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, the "Marsal Tito" Barracks were still occupied by the JNA. The negotiations were not progressing very satisfactorily because General Mladic was reluctant to meet Presidency demands to hand over a quantity of small arms as part of the price of facilitating the release of the JNA forces. He had a very firm position that that should not take place, and this was, in effect, stalling the agreement to achieve the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph 76 of your statement, you mention a meeting you attended the next day, the 29th of May, 1992, with General Boskovic, Colonel Cadjo, and Lieutenant-Colonel Jankovic. What did General Boskovic tell you in relation to the attack the night before?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Before we -- before he answers that, I would like to just express some concern by the way this statement is being used by this witness. I think that it is not proper for the witness to be referring to his written statement unless he needs to to refresh his memory, but each question is directing him to the paragraph of the statement, he's then looking at it and giving his answer, and I don't think that's a proper way to proceed. So I think that we ought to proceed in the way in which he answers the questions -- I think the reference to the statement is helpful for the rest of us to follow, but he shouldn't be reviewing the statement prior to giving the answer unless he needs to to refresh his recollection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, if you can answer without referring to your statement, that's possible. But if you need to, you can do so with our leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll try and do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please. Let's proceed. Can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So what did General Boskovic tell you in relation to the attack on the night of the 28th of May?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, that meeting was particularly notable, in that the representatives from the Presidency brought to the meeting a tape of a radio intercept of General Mladic directing the fire of his artillery units the previous night, the night of the 28th. The tape was in Serbo-Croat, so -- and I don't speak that language, so I don't know what the exact contents of the tape were, other than what both parties, both the Presidency and the JNA representatives, had told me. They told me that it was Mladic directing fire against various parts of the city. They intimated that there was no need for that sort of fire. They thought that he was acting irresponsibly and that he was out of control. They did not support his actions. General Boskovic apologised to me for the behaviour of General Mladic and made it quite clear that the JNA did not support these actions. It was quite clear to me that all members at that meeting thought the shelling of the night before was quite extraordinary and unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph 77, you mention a meeting with Mladic which occurred on the following day, the 30th of May, 1992, wherein you conveyed the Secretary-General's appeal to Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I had a meeting with General Mladic on that day. It was part, I believe, of a multi-pronged effort to impress upon the Bosnian Serbs the necessity to moderate their behaviour in regard to their activity against Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can I have 65 ter 09574 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly invited to sit closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Before that document comes up, what -- so the Secretary-General's appeal to Mladic was to do what, in particular?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It was to moderate or to lessen the attacks against the city. It called for restraint and was, I believe, followed up by a Security Council resolution which called for an opening of the Sarajevo Airport for the delivery of humanitarian supplies and demilitarisation of parts of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document that's on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I do. It's a -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I should tell, for the record, Ms. Sutherland, it's 9574, the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. That's what I thought I'd said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think this is a document that I recognise. This is not a document that I've seen before.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How did General Mladic respond when you spoke with him?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: General Mladic was once again simply saying that this was simply defending the Serb people, defending themselves against attack, and that it was important to have the release of the JNA from the barracks. He was -- as I understand it, at this meeting he was unaware or was not prepared to acknowledge the fact that Mr. Karadzic may have made an agreement to allow humanitarian aid to come in through a UN-controlled airport in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know whether there was -- whether the Secretary-General ever issued a press release in relation to his appeal?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can I have 65 ter 06219 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: General, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I do recognise it. That's the resolution I was referring to which had motivated the meetings on the 30th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 of that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I can draw your attention to the paragraph starting: "Deeply concerned that those UNPROFOR personnel remaining in Sarajevo have been subjected to deliberate mortar and small-arms fire ..." Is this consistent to what you had reported to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes. As I indicated earlier, I had reported formally on my command net to General Nambiar about the number of attacks that had been directed against UN forces moving about the city, and this is a reflection of the concern that he and UN New York felt about those attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I seek to tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1031, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: General, I wish to turn to the topic of detention facilities which is detailed in paragraphs 101 to 104 of your statement. In paragraph 101, you stated that there were reports at the time that each side was running their own detention camps. How did you receive this information?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I received that information from both parties, alleging activities by the other party, and also formally in writing from the Presidency, in the form of a list and a formal protest from Mr. Halilovic, who was then the Presidency defence minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You also state, in paragraph 101, that during the airport negotiations, you raised allegations of large-scale detention of civilians with Biljana Plavsic and that Radovan Karadzic was present during this conversation. That's noted in paragraph 102. What information did you provide to them about the allegations that you'd received?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I'd received an allegation from the Presidency representatives that there was a tunnel somewhere to the south of Sarajevo which was being used to hold a large number of non-Serb people, many of them women and children, and the Presidency were concerned about the safety of these people. And I had asked Mrs. Plavsic if this was true, and her response was that, yes, it was, and that there were a number of detention camps, but they simply held males of military age who were being taken out of the -- out of circulation so they couldn't join the fighting. She said that they were well treated and if I wished, I could go to the site and visit that tunnel location at a later date. I have to say that I followed up on that offer to go and visit those people or to visit that site. However, when we were finally given approval, we were told that it was some considerable distance out of Sarajevo, that our safety could not be assured. Also, because it was out of our UN communications range and there was no possibility of being able to assist any of my troops who were sent there, that there were plenty of other activities for us to be involved in, in the end I did not send a party down to visit that camp or that detention centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I can turn now to the airport negotiations. In paragraph 90 of your statement, you stated that the airport agreement was signed on the 5th of June, 1992. Who signed the agreement for the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have Rule 65 ter 08640 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I do. It's a document jointly drafted between myself and Mr. Thornberry, the chief political officer of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we can just go to the second page. And the last page. I seek to tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is the only original one? English is the original?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: General?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, it was all done in English. We had very limited interpreter capability at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1032, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And can you just explain to the Chamber, the fact that it has Mr. Karadzic's signature on this document and Cedric Thornberry's signature, but not the Bosnian government representative's signature, why is that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: The Bosnian government's position, both in 1992 and 1993, was that they would not meet directly with the Serb leadership. They wouldn't be in the same room, they wouldn't sign the same document. So it was necessary to use shuttle diplomacy and also to get them to sign separate copies of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. That document can be taken off the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You have also mentioned, at corrected paragraph 91 of your statement, that there was heavy shelling on the 6th of June, the day after the airport agreement was signed. Can you briefly describe the nature of this fighting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: The fighting was mainly concentrated around the airport, Dobrinja, Nedzarici, that sort of area. It was very heavy fighting, involving extensive use of artillery. By the sound of it, a lot of infantry soldiers were involved. It appeared to be both sides attempting to gain tactical advantage of ground which overlooked and perhaps controlled the airport, now that it had been agreed that the airport would pass to the control of the UN. That fighting continued more or less unabated until the 24th of June, when I left the city. It was General MacKenzie's position that before the airport agreement could be implemented, there needed to be a period of 48 hours where the cease-fire, which had been agreed by both parties, actually came into effect. He was never successful in achieving that at least before the 24th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can I have 65 ter 10601 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: General Wilson, you authenticate this document, in paragraph 60 of your statement, as being authored by you. I'd like to direct your attention to paragraph 9. If we could go to the next page, please. Note 9 says: "Today there has been very heavy fighting in Sarajevo and the CMO estimates significant loss of life." If we could just go back to the first page, I'm sorry, so we can see the date of this document. This is dated the 8th of June, 1992. So what did you mean in that paragraph 9 by "significant loss of life"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Firstly, if I can explain that this is a cable sent back to my national authorities. I was required to do that on a weekly basis. It's an administrative report which allows them to assess the security situation there and the sensibility of leaving me there in UN service. And I'm stating there that on the 8th of June, three days after the airport agreement, there had been particularly heavy fighting around Sarajevo, so heavy as to give me the impression there had to be significant loss of life.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I seek to tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P1033.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can I have 65 ter 10603 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: General, again do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It's another weekly sitrep dated the 23rd of June back to my national authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And this is referred to in paragraph 60 of your statement. If we can go to paragraph numbered 1, and this is dated the 23rd of June, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: "This past week has been marked by heavy fighting in Sarajevo. Serb forces have continued to shell the city and, in particular, have initiated a concentrated attack to capture the suburb of Dobrinja, adjacent to the airport. The attack has been supported by artillery and tanks. A mortar attack on a crowded old city street on the 22nd of June, 1992, resulted in 14 dead and 35 wounded." Again, who was responsible for this concentrated attack?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: You need to be more specific, counsellor. Which particular attack are we talking about, the mortar attack, or are we talking about the shelling of the city, or are we talking about --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, in relation to the concentrated attack on the suburb of Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's hard to say exactly. It was my belief at the time that the Serb forces were trying to clean out any Presidency forces that might be in the vicinity of the airport so that they would be able to influence the security and the tactical situation around the airport. However, you could also say that the fighting may have been initiated by the Presidency forces, who were attempting to achieve the same aim. It's impossible to say who was responsible for the attack. Both of them certainly participated most vigorously. But the great majority of fire-power is in favour of the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And do you recall now, in relation to the mortar attack on the old city street, who was responsible for that attack?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: This attack took place in the context of continued Serb mortar fire into the city, Serb artillery fire into the city. I'm unaware of whether a formal investigation was ever conducted into that unfortunate incident and whether any attribution was made.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I seek to tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1034, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that document can be removed from the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: General, in your statement, at paragraph 43, you state that from what you observed, the Presidency forces were armed only with small arms, and, in paragraph 50, that the Presidency troops did not have a great number of weapons. You have talked a little about it already, but can you describe the disparity in terms of the calibre of weapons, the heavy weapons between the Presidency forces and the Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: The Presidency forces had only a small number of mortars, very few artillery pieces, two or three tanks, to the best of my knowledge at this time. The Serb forces investing the city, on the other hand, had a large number of heavy weapons, many different varieties. My estimate would be they had at least 200 barrels of mortars and artillery which they could use against the city. We're talking about maybe a dozen heavy weapons on the part of the Presidency forces, and 200 or more with the Serbs, in my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, finally, in your professional opinion, were the Bosnian Serb responses to threats posed by the BiH government forces proportionate?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: They were, in my belief, disproportionate, widespread, and inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, that completes my examination-in-chief. I seek to tender into evidence all of the remaining associated exhibits listed in Appendix A to the Rule 92 notification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By way of example, some of them -- at least one of them had been already admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The last item.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The report, the analysis of the combat readiness and activities of the Army of Republika Srpska in 1992. That's Exhibit D325, so I don't seek to have that admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are there any objections, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. With respect to the documents described in paragraph 79 through 82 of the statement, which is 65 ter 09573 and 01072, these are documents that didn't involve the witness. But on paragraph 81, he commented by saying that: "I can state they appear to be typical UNPROFOR documents that are consistent with events of that time." They involve meetings at which he was not present, and we don't think that those are appropriately admitted through this witness, nor do they form an integral part of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But he referred to those documents in his statement, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, he referred to the documents in his statement, but the only comment he had about them was that they appear to be typical UNPROFOR documents and are consistent with the events of that time. So you can take any witness and show him materials which he didn't participate and had no personal knowledge, and he could say that's consistent and that's a typical UNPROFOR document, but that doesn't make the documents admissible, in my view. In particular, he was talking about a meeting with President Milosevic, where he wasn't present, and then another meeting with Dr. Karadzic, where he wasn't present. And I simply don't think there's a sufficient link between his testimony and knowledge and these pieces of evidence that these should be admitted through his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then would you like the witness to go through those two documents and then testify as to what he knows about those to documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: If he knows something more than what he's stated in his statement, then maybe that would be useful for the Prosecution. But if all he could say is there were typical UNPROFOR documents and they're consistent with his opinion at the time, I don't think that's relevant and doesn't add anything for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, do you have any observations?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can call the witness -- the documents up and discuss them with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's do that, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 09573 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Before that comes onto the screen: General, when you had your meeting with General Mladic on the 30th of May, 1992, were you aware -- or was any other meeting going on with other leaders in relation to the attacks on the city of Sarajevo in the days surrounding the 30th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: On the 30th of May, I was unaware of any other meetings taking place on this matter. Subsequently, I became aware of them, because Mr. Thornberry, when he arrived in Sarajevo on the 2nd of June, gave me the background to the negotiations to which we were about to undertake and the fact that there had been other meetings taking place in the past few days. So in saying that I was familiar with this sort of document that was shown to me by you, counsellor, I was aware of the general content of them, but not the detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, has this -- in my view, a sufficient nexus has been shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness is aware of the situation, the content is consistent with his knowledge, and he was aware of the document. We admit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1035, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if I could have Rule 65 ter 01072 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is referred to in your statement at paragraph 80, General. Are you able to give the Court any more insight into this document and any knowledge that you may have had in relation to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Can we screen down a bit more, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's a document I've previously been shown, and it's -- once again, it's a report on the negotiations that General Morillon was conducting. And, once again, I was briefed on the general nature of these negotiations by Cedric Thornberry when he came down so I could effectively participate in the negotiations for the opening up of the airport.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I seek to tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1036, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that concludes your examination-in-chief, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The other associated exhibit will be admitted, and the Registrar, in due course, will assign the exhibit numbers and circulate them to the parties. Judge Morrison has a question for you, General, before Mr. Karadzic starts his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. No doubt, Dr. Karadzic may raise the same question, but I just want to make sure it's answered before I forget it. General, in respect of what you call the Presidency forces, you said earlier in your testimony that they had maybe a dozen or so heavy weapons. Were those weapons that you saw, yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did see some of those weapons later when they were brought under observation of UNPROFOR as part of the demilitarisation of the airport, but I'm really referring to my observation of outgoing fire from the city which you could hear, and it was very limited. You can hear the primary noise of a weapon being fired out of the city, and there was very little evidence of that. I did see there was a mortar position established near the PTT building one time by the Presidency forces, who were using us as cover. I did see a mobile mortar once. When I was visiting the Presidency, once I heard mortar fire being fired out from the vicinity of there, but it was not a great weight of fire, and that's why I say their capacity was very limited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: You mention mortars. Could you assess the calibre of the mortar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm assuming they'd be 82-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And any long-barrelled artillery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe they had a few pieces of long-barrelled artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the time, shall we take the break now? We'll have a break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I take it that you can start. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Excuse me, Mr. President. After I addressed you this morning, I uncovered yet another disclosure violation of the material that Mr. Reid was kind enough to send me by e-mail, and this is an October 11th, 2008, report of interview with this witness that is clearly 66(A)(2) material which, by order of the Trial Chamber, had to be disclosed to us by the 7th of May, 2009. And we just received it -- I actually just received it this morning, but it was apparently included in a CD that was given over on the 17th of June to Dr. Karadzic. And so I think now we have three specific violations of disclosure rules with respect to this witness. I would ask that you make a ruling as to each of them and then give us some remedy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was provided with the copy of that disclosure batch, but could you identify what number it is, the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's included in Batch 287. There's two documents in that. This is an information report. The ERN number is 0642-9017. It's a three-page document dated the 11th of October, 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was referring to 66(A)(2) material, the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I've just -- that's exactly what I've just described to you as the -- that 66(A)(2) material is in Batch 287. It's an OTP information report dated the 11th of October, 2008, and it bears the ERN number that I've just read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I couldn't find it. Do you have the document with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have it electronically. I could send it to you, to Ram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Disclosure Batch 287. I was looking at Disclosure Batch 289, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I haven't even had a chance to look at 289 yet. I note there's four items that are authored by the witness, but I haven't had a chance to look at that yet. I'm now referring to this item that's in batch 287.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a copy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have the explanation, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour. It's unfortunate that this information report wasn't disclosed to the accused earlier. However, the date of the information report is subsequent to the information report being taken in October 2008. A consolidated statement was taken from the witness in March 2009. The information report that Mr. Robinson is referring to is contained on the cover page of Mr. Wilson's statement, which is now P01029, and it's also mentioned in paragraph 1 of that consolidated statement. Paragraph 2 of his consolidated statement states that the statement is a consolidation of the previous testimony and statements, as well as additional observation and references. So the information that's contained in the information report of October 2008 is, in fact, included in another form in the consolidated statement which was taken from the witness in 2009. So in my submission, the accused suffers no prejudice from the non-disclosure or the late disclosure of the information report. If Your Honour would like to see the information report, I have it here, and a copy of the correspondence. Your Honour, can I just add that we have put into train two additional mechanisms, also following on from Your Honours' decision last week, in order to capture any outstanding Rule 66(A)(2) materials in relation to any of the forthcoming witnesses. Two separate but related mechanisms have been put into place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. Mr. Robinson and Mr. Karadzic, while we understand your concerns, and the Chamber is also concerned about the late disclosure, but with respect to this time, I don't think the disclosure of additional documents would be such that would require the accused to postpone his cross-examination at all. So the Chamber is of the opinion that the accused can start his cross-examination now, and we can see, at the end of his cross-examination, whether he needs additional time because of this late disclosure. That said, we'll start. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you, General Wilson. First of all, I'd like to express my gratitude to you for having been so kind as to receive my dear pro bono associate, Professor Kevin Heller, and to co-operate with the Defence, which is certainly of assistance to us, and it is to your credit. So thank you for that. Now, General, sir, you were, well, as a colonel, in Sarajevo during a very important time; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Certainly, a very interesting time, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree with me when I say that those first two years, especially 1992, that that was the most intensive year in terms of the number of events that took place?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I was only in Bosnia in 1992 and associated with the problem of the former Yugoslavia in 1993. What happened after that, I don't know, so I can't make that value judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today, you were among the first witnesses to talk about the very heavy fighting and difficult fighting. Do you agree that for heavy fighting to take place, you need two sides?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, you do need two sides to have heavy fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And would you also agree that apart from the forces which the Muslim side had in town, that part of the 1st Corps was at Mount Igman and in the surrounding parts of Sarajevo as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I don't know what the 1st Corps is, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know that the Muslim forces in Sarajevo were called the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you saw something of the weapons before they came under the control of UNPROFOR, and you also saw some after UNPROFOR took control. Is it possible that there were weapons which you did not see?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The agreement -- the airport agreement was that heavy weapons within range of the airport needed to be placed under UNPROFOR control or observation, so it's quite possible that both parties had weapons of different varieties outside range and they would not be subject to the agreed regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the fact that the Muslims in town had mortars, I assume static ones, and you also mentioned having seen and heard of mortars placed on trucks, flatbed trucks; is that correct? That is to say, that at Serb positions and in the Serbian parts of town, they opened fire from mortars placed on trucks?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: In your question, you say that mortars are, by nature, static. In fact, by nature, they're highly mobile. That's their great asset. They can be moved quickly. So I can't say I ever saw any static mortars. I did see mortars in different places and assumed they were being moved about. And, yes, I did -- once a mortar mounted on the back of a truck, I observed that from the PTT, I observed it fire two or three rounds, and I saw the weight of fire that the Serb forces fired in response. That fire was indiscriminate and disproportionate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You confirmed, yourself, that the Muslim forces used the presence or, rather, the installations and facilities of the United Nations as a mask for opening fire; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's correct. And when we raised our objections with the appropriate authorities, those weapons were removed from the vicinity of the PTT.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I put it to you that this happened in 1993 and 1994 and 1995, would you accept that, that this would be repeated? They were removed, but then they were positioned close to you afterwards?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of what happened in 1994 or 1995, nor any means of finding out. And I was well placed within the United Nations reporting chain in 1993 to receive and be made aware of such reports, and I have no recollection of a repeat of the Presidency forces placing weaponry under the cover of the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that they positioned their weapons near the radar and other UN installations, and that the UN officers had to protest because of that and to demand that they be moved to a distance of at least 500 metres away?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I'm unaware of that, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have now called up on e-court 1D01275, please. It's a document dated the 28th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Hosen? Is he familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I have no recollection of Mr. Hosen. It's got "General Hosen" on the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about General Siber; do you know him?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I have a vague recollection of Mr. Siber. Perhaps a member of the Presidency forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, would you take a look at the contents of this document in translation and tell me whether it corresponds to this distance of 500 metres, or, rather, that General Hosen is demanding and asking for co-operation and understanding that this be carried out? Is that consistent with what you know about the positioning of those artillery weapons close to your installations, artillery pieces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: The document certainly refers to the placing of weapons within 500 metres, but I'm unaware, sir, of this particular incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And does that conform with what you know about the situation and with what you said in connection with the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, I already indicated to you, Mr. Karadzic, I'm unaware of the situation, so I can't really comment upon it. I can simply confirm that in 1992, there was an incident where the Presidency forces placed a mortar position under cover of the PTT. They fired from there. When we raised our objection with the relevant Presidency forces, they could see that this was inappropriate action on behalf of -- on part of their forces, and they effected the removal of it. We're talking about two different incidents, one I have absolutely no knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that Nedzarici is a purely Serb settlement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I'm unaware of the ethnic distribution within Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You lived near Nedzarici, opposite Nedzarici, in fact; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I did live in Nedzarici, but I didn't ask people what ethnic -- of what ethnicity they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you do agree, don't you, that it was the Serbs who controlled Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: At what point of time are we talking about? I mean, the possession of parts of Sarajevo changed from time to time. If you can state a time-frame, I can give an opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But Nedzarici, from start -- from the beginning to the end, were under Serb control, because it's a Serb settlement and it was held by the inhabitants of Nedzarici, themselves. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I was unaware that it was a Serb settlement. And my understanding was that the settlement of Nedzarici and, indeed, Dobrinja was contested by both parties, and the confrontation line changed over time in that area. It was one of the heavily contested parts of Sarajevo, particularly in the period May/June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we look at what it says here: "Today, some three French soldiers were seriously wounded in Nedzarici." Is it reasonable to understand that somebody shot at Nedzarici, as a Serb suburb, and that the French soldiers were wounded there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I can't speculate what happened there because I simply was not there. I have no recollection of this incident, nor am I able to recall any reports about it. Perhaps it satisfies you for me to say that there were many of these types of incident involving all three parties during 1992 and, indeed, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, you weren't in other places in town either, whereas you say you know that there was shooting, and you even think that they were civilians targets that were targeted. Now, do you think that the Nedzarici settlement was a civilian target?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Nedzarici was -- in my belief, was a -- yeah, an urban area consisting of apartment blocks where people resided and continued to reside during 1992. There was fighting in the area, and both sides were involved.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to tender this document now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having looked at the document, General, do you now remember General Hosen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We would object, Your Honour. There's no nexus being shown to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The General didn't confirm anything about this document, he's not aware of this document, so we'll not admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it says here -- well, General Hosen mentions the incident. It says: [In English] "Three days ago, some relation of 200 metres distance from our facilities --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we gave our ruling, and you'll have another opportunity to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then next time, before your ruling, I shall ask for the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, did you know that the Muslim side used other facilities too in order to make the Serb side respond, such as hospitals, for example?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: You'll need to clarify the question for me, Mr. Karadzic. I'm unclear as to what you mean by "used other facilities."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you confirmed yourself that during your visit to the Presidency, there was fire coming from the vicinity of the Presidency building; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I tell you that that happened, for the most part, when some high-ranking guests came to visit the Presidency to provoke a Serb response, does that sound reasonable to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, it does sound reasonable to me. And it was also very successful, because it inevitably resulted in some response; heavy fire from the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So do you agree, and you mentioned this yourself, that the mortars, placed on trucks, also provoked -- or, rather, fired at civilian targets, because after the firing the truck was removed and then you would have the Serb response, and it would appear that there were no artillery pieces or weapons in the area when that response came?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It would not have been possible for me to know what the target of outgoing Presidency mortar fire was because it was outside the city. I could perhaps hear the primary sound of the round being fired, but I'd be unaware of the target that it was actually hitting. The second part of your question infers that it was done deliberately to draw fire into civilian areas. I don't know what the motive was of the Presidency forces. The reality is it did draw disproportionate and widespread response from the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that UNPROFOR was concerned because of the positioning of Muslim artillery in the vicinity of the hospital, for example, and that they protested?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I am generally aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have 1D1854 called up on e-court, please. I think that you've all received it. It was announced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you take a look at this document now, please. It's a letter from General Morillon to Mr. Izetbegovic, the president of the Presidency or rump Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, the contents, are they familiar to you, and does it comply with what you know about shooting at sensitive targets close to? May we take a look at the whole document? Could the general be allowed to see the whole document? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I have not seen this document before, and I would have no need to see it in my position then in Geneva. However, it seems consistent with some of the oral reports I received out of Sarajevo that this type of activity took place from time to time. And --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. General, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. And it does address an issue that was of concern to the UN, not only in Sarajevo but in other places, that mortar positions were set up by Presidency forces in areas prohibited under the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you remember whether you were aware of the fact -- well, is this document admitted into evidence? Let me ask that first, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D328, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you remember that you were conscious of the fact that the Muslim side hoped there would be military -- international military intervention, and do you agree that things like this could cause and bring about a military intervention in their opinion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
