utterances.text: I can't say what the wishes and hopes of the Presidency may have been in regard to international intervention, whether it be military or otherwise. Certainly, there was a -- in May and June of 1992, there was a hope and a wish that the media attention that was given to the tragic events in Sarajevo would engender some international support and sympathy for the Presidency. Now, the issue here about placing weapons in an inappropriate place or having roving mortars around the city ignores the fact that the response that these provoked was entirely disproportionate. You might have two rounds of mortar fire being directed out of the city, and there would be 200 rounds of heavy-calibre artillery fired in response, covering a large area. So it's important to understand that while provocative conduct had been perhaps perpetrated by one side, the response was entirely disproportionate to the threat that was engendered by this activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the answer was a bit lengthier than I had expected, but therefore the redirect is going to be shorter. So thank you, General. When somebody declares war on you, is it legitimate to win?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: One, of course, hopes to win, but it's legitimate to fight.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1D1852, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, tell me, General, what is the point of a proportionate response? I'm not a soldier; I am -- actually, I don't know anything about military institutions. But what is the point of a proportionate response? Is it to keep the conflict going forever or what?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Proportionate response is in the context of the Geneva Conventions. If you're going to fire into an area and cause collateral damage or civilian casualties, you have to be absolutely certain that the amount of force and the type of force you're using is proportionate to the threat and that it is also appropriate for those particular circumstances. For example, there are other more accurate means of fire that could have removed that threat of a roving mortar. Anti-aircraft weapons used in a direct ground role are highly accurate, and with the observation allowed to the Serb forces in the high ground overlooking Sarajevo, it would have been possible to use similar-type weapons which are highly accurate to engage specific targets. The other issue here, as a soldier, in my experience, if you are going to be involved in conflict where there is a risk of collateral damage or civilian casualties, then you would have with you a military lawyer who is an expert in the Conventions and who would provide advice to you on whether a target should be engaged and with what type of fire. Whether the Serb forces took this precaution, I don't know. The evidence is that they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I ask you from where you were observing these incidents, this fire from the PTT building; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: You could look out the window in some incidents. Otherwise, the roof afforded quite a broad view of the terrain and the city around the PTT, certainly more than a kilometre in each direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How far away is the PTT building from the center of the city, if we take Skenderija and the Hygiene Institute and perhaps Marin Dvor to be the center?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I don't have a detailed knowledge of Sarajevo, as I indicated to you. I was there for some six weeks. We only ventured outside the PTT on specific missions because of the security threat. I'm more aware of the area around the PTT. I travelled often to the city. I don't know exactly how far it is; some kilometres, certainly more than you could observe from the PTT. If you're -- I simply do not have such a detailed knowledge of the city that I can talk about specific suburbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know what the deployment was of the Muslim forces in town, itself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I didn't. My belief at the time was they had such few forces and, in particular, such few weapons that any military forces they had would have needed to have been deployed on the confrontation line, that they wouldn't have had spare forces to deploy in depth to thicken up their defence. So my assumption was, other than some troops who may have been resting or the odd logistic facility, all of their military forces would have been deployed on the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I tell you that only within the town itself they had two or three times more soldiers than the Serbs did, would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I find that hard to believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you agree that mortars and artillery were not kept at the confrontation line, but further back?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: By their nature, mortar and artillery are deployed in depth behind the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's what you say of tanks as well; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Not necessarily. Tanks are a direct-fire weapon which need to actually observe the target. And to fire directly, they can't fire over buildings or over physical features, so they are quite often deployed well forward or immediately behind the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at this document? At the time, you were working for the conference as an adviser to the mediators; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: In April 1993, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll down a bit? Can we have a look at the lower part of paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General Mladic says: [In English] "Importantly he stated during the discussions, that the solution to the Serbian situation would be a political and not a military one." [Interpretation] Do you remember that Mladic was in favour of a political solution for Srebrenica rather than a military one?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Can we scroll to the top of that document again, please? When I look at this document, I can't recall that particular meeting in Sarajevo, and I believe that this is a report passed to me, as the UNPROFOR liaison officer in Geneva, and that I am then passing this information from Geneva to Vance and Owen, who were then located in New York. In summary, I was not at that meeting. I am simply passing information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that we had stopped our counter-offensive near Srebrenica and that that year we did not enter Srebrenica at all?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I'm only vaguely aware of that, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 2, please, page 2 of this document, paragraph number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I please ask you to read the beginning of paragraph 4?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: "The force commander also believes that yesterday's --" Do you want me to read aloud or -- "... yesterday's shelling of Srebrenica and Sarajevo were provoked by the Muslim forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please read on, if that's not a problem?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Of course: "Given the apparent Muslim determination to ensure that the cease-fire is not effective and to maintain Srebrenica in the world headlines, it is hard to see how the force commander can successfully bring the two sides together. The force commander has, at his level, brought all appropriate pressure to bear on the Serb side, and has at least been able to extricate a commitment for participation in military talks. President Izetbegovic is apparently absent in Saudi Arabia and has not, therefore, been able to bring his influence to bear on his military commander. The president's co-operation cannot, however, be expected unless some pressure is brought to bear."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The last sentence: [In English] "The president's co-operation cannot, however, be expected unless some pressure is brought to bear." [Interpretation] Do you agree that this report also speaks of the fact that pressure is being brought to bear only against the Serb side and that nothing can be achieved if pressure is not exerted on the Muslim side as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the whole point of this cable is to co-opt Mr. Vance and Lord Owen into putting pressure on the Muslim side, to get some agreement. That's the whole point of it, to bring pressure to bear on the other party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there any such pressure while you were in Bosnia in 1992 and 1993? And while you were part of the conference, was there equal pressure brought to bear against the Muslim side as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's a very broad question. You'd need to be time specific. My involvement in negotiating with senior political and military leadership in 1992 was mainly in the period of May/June, and then subsequently over Dubrovnik and the no-fly zone. And then, of course, in 1993 I was an observer in Geneva of the negotiations there, and I'm aware that pressure was brought at the conference, internationally and in every other way, on all three participants in the conflict in Yugoslavia to come to some sort of agreement. It was not just the Serbs who were being pressured, but also the Croats and the Presidency of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this in line with what you had also noted; namely, that the Muslim side is committed to ensuring that Srebrenica is in the headlines?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure what that question means, Mr. Karadzic. Could you rephrase it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, today you confirmed that they were interested in shooting near the hospital and other facilities of yours so that they would win sympathy and so that they would be on the front pages of world media. Also, it says here in this document that cease-fires do not go on because the Muslim side wants to be in the world headlines; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I don't know why the Muslim forces placed firing units near the hospital or other facilities, as you allege. I can't look into their motivation, whether it was to gain media attention or some tactical advantage. It's impossible to sensibly comment upon that. And with regard to cease-fires, I have to say that you can't blame any particular side in the conflict in the former Yugoslavia for breaking cease-fires. All three parties did it with gay abandon for the two years that I was associated with the conflict there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get to that, because the United Nations actually came to some different information. I'm interested in the following now: Does this telegram confirm that their interest was, as stated in paragraph 4, to remain in world headlines; Right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That was the force commander's opinion, having met -- as a result of that meeting, and I am simply passing that view on to the co-chairmen in New York.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, but I was told that the previous document, 1D1854, which was admitted as D328, was identical to the last page of Exhibit D99, so instead we'll use that number to this document. So this document will be admitted as Exhibit D328 instead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that that is not correct. So far, we haven't shown Morillon's document. Oh, yes, that does seem to be the case, actually. Thank you. 1D946, could we have that, please. I believe that there is a translation of this document, so could we please have the English version as well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at this document? I don't think it's necessary for us to read it. This is a special combat report for the 28th of July, 1993. The Command of Tactical Group Vogosca is providing information to their superior commands as to what is happening. Could you please cast a glance at this? They say here that Miladin Cukovic, a well-known physician was killed. All of Sarajevo knew him. Is this event consistent with what we had discussed a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I'm unaware of this incident, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, as something that had happened, as a phenomenon, does it correspond to what you know had been going on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we do not need the speculation on the part of the witness or his opinion. He said he didn't know about this incident. Let's move on to your next topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then you're not going to admit this at all, if I understand things correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it it has already been admitted. No, I was confused with your numbering. You are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, for starters, can we try to deal with things a bit more concisely? Let us see what you could have known in Sarajevo. Could you have known of certain things happening on both sides?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: In July 1993, I received operational reports from UNPROFOR on daily activities. I was also privy to all sensitive traffic, that's message traffic, between New York and Zagreb or UNPROFOR headquarters, and most of the higher-level sensitive reporting within UNPROFOR. This sort of incident would have probably been mentioned in the daily operational report, but I have no recollection of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That means that it would have been mentioned in the reports if the reports were objective; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, there's a supposition there that the reports weren't objective. The operational reports, in my view, were objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to that period, though. You came in the beginning of March 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Correct -- January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Right, January. That's even better. Now, General, are you aware of what had happened in that period of time up until the 24th of June, when you left?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: In what regard, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For example, did you know that there was a conference on Bosnia-Herzegovina that was underway?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes. I believe it was done under the auspices of the European Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's right, that's right, it was the European Community at the time. Do you know what was happening in the Neretva River Valley at the time? Do you know that Serbs were the victims down there and that they fled from the Neretva Valley?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Are we talking about January 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no. February, March, up to April.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: My understanding of the movement of ethnic communities within Bosnia was that in March/April it was the Muslims who were being cleaned out of Northern Bosnia. I'm unaware that any Muslim activity took place in the -- you said the Neretva Valley, to clear out ethnic Serbs. I'm just unaware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that 44.000 Serbs lived in the Neretva Valley, Mostar included?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that almost all of them were expelled and that they all went to Nevesinje and other Serb areas, the so-called High Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I'm unaware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that before April, Serbs had fled from Livno, most of the Serbs had fled from Livno?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know which armed incidents had occurred before the war broke out? We're talking about Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Despite your plea for brevity, I have to now say that prior to the 8th of March, 1992, the focus of my military liaison mission was on Croatia and the UN -- what became the UNPAs. I was not even vaguely aware of what was happening down in Bosnia. In March, when I deployed to -- or by the time I deployed to Sarajevo on the 22nd of March, it was clear that there were ethnic tensions across Northern Bosnia. Now, the directive that had been issued to the military observers, as part of UNPROFOR, as I'd indicated earlier in my evidence, was that they would deploy to the Bihac and the Mostar areas, which were areas that had been noted as being particularly sensitive to -- or there was potential for ethnic tension there, so I'm broadly aware that there was some problems down in Mostar. And we did, in fact, during late March, early April deploy observers down there for a short period, but the fighting was so intense that we actually had to withdraw them after only seven days or ten days, something like that. We actually had a couple of our observers wounded, and they were unable to perform their duties. So they were withdrawn for safety reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please look at 1D1308.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for it to appear on the screens: Since you were in Croatia until the 8th of March, are you aware of the fact that on the 3rd of March, the army moved from Croatia to Bosanski Brod, killing some Serbs there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Which army are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe those were the Zengas, the National Guard Corps, or other irregulars that existed in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I'm unaware of that activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you obtain your information only from your observers, and are you aware only of the events that occurred in the areas that they covered, or did you have other sources too?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: We had a broad range of sources; media, other agencies operating in the area, other elements of UNPROFOR, the local population. Each of the parties would like to tell us what the other party was doing. There were a broad range of sources of information available, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can we please look at this document? This is a letter sent by the late Professor Koljevic, who was a member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and later on of Republika Srpska, and he also became at one point the vice-president of Republika Srpska. This is a letter penned by Professor Koljevic, addressed to Ambassador Cutileiro. Could you please have a look at this letter? Do you know that at that time, and at least from the 22nd of February, we had already agreed on a declaration or a statement regarding the principles for the solution of the crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which later became what is known as the Lisbon Agreement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic, I had no knowledge of the politics or events in Bosnia prior to about the 22nd of March, when my UNPROFOR -- my Military Observers' headquarters was deployed to Sarajevo, and I was not involved in any of the negotiations between UNPROFOR and any of the parties until the departure of UNPROFOR headquarters on about the 16th and 17th of May. And I was certainly not in the information loop for whatever the negotiators from the European Union may have been doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you did obtain some information. You knew where you were going and you knew what was going on in that country to which you were being sent; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's very sad to admit, but I was not aware, nor do I think the force commander, General Nambiar, was aware, nor the chief political officer, Mr. Thornberry, were fully aware of what was about to happen in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The focus of UNPROFOR, when it deployed to the former Yugoslavia, was on Croatia, with the exception of the military observers who were deployed to Bihac and Mostar. That's the sad reality of how the international community saw the situation prior to March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But this is the 4th or the 5th of April, 1992, the 4th or the 5th of April, and you can see that there are 2500 Serb refugees from Kupres, and the events in Bijeljina had already happened, as had those in Bosanski Brod. And Professor Koljevic is trying, in the face of all those conflicts so that this is what he says: "Despite the unfortunate conflicts, we would like to have some peace -- to see a peaceful solution for the warring factions." Do you see that? It's in the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. And in April 1992, there was some limited fighting taking place in Sarajevo, and it was broadly known that there was ethnic cleansing taking place and that there was quite serious conflict outside Sarajevo. But these were emerging events, as far as UNPROFOR was concerned. UNPROFOR was suddenly having to negotiate with members of the Bosnian political leadership, and I include Serb, Croats, and Muslim parties in that, while the focus was meant to be on deploying a force of 25.000 people to the UNPAs in Croatia. They were not in any way involved in the political negotiations being run by the European Union. I can't comment any more on this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you see here that Professor Koljevic reminds -- or, rather, informs Ambassador Cutileiro that the Muslim side has taken measures to establish its own Territorial Defence, which has nothing to do with the Yugoslav People's Army, and it was an unlegal [as interpreted] move?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I'm not what you -- what you mean by an illegal move.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Territorial Defence was subordinate to the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you see here that Professor Koljevic says that the Muslim side, the Muslim side, despite the fact that there are three constituent peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you can see here in the penultimate paragraph it says that they are trying to organise a nucleus of a new Bosnian army while waiting for the recognition?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I can see it's written there under sub-point 3, in that paragraph. Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you see that Professor Koljevic is concerned that the Serbs would not join the new force and that this was the situation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I can see that Mr. Koljevic is trying to communicate that, yes. But I'm not sure of the relevance of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the relevance is in the fact that you had come to the country as a military expert, as a military observer, and these are military activities, eminently so. Were you aware of those military activities, and did you understand that these were, in effect, preparations for a war?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'll restate my evidence from earlier that UNPROFOR's mandate, in March, April, and May of 1992, was in Croatia, that the headquarters was simply located in Sarajevo. The only people who had a mission at all in Bosnia were my military observers. It was not the business of the force commander to involve himself in these matters. UNPROFOR did not get a mandate in Bosnia until the airport agreement was effected. Prior to that, the military observers would deploy people in Bihac and Mostar. What was happening in Sarajevo was something that was imposed upon the force commander and his officers, and they were trying to get some sort of understanding of what was happening. They were unaware of the detail of what the three parties were doing, whether they were raising forces or not. I have said in my statement that I had received reports primarily from Croatian military sources that the Serb authorities in Bosnia, in January of 1992, were disarming the Muslims and arming the Serb elements in Northern Bosnia, and I covered that in my statement. That was just information we'd received, and that was, in part, confirmed by JNA command, that this was happening. It seems to me that the only concrete evidence that I have that people had been making military preparations and raising military forces were the Serb side. I saw no evidence that the Bosnian Presidency forces were ready for conflict in January or May of 1992. I'd say clearly they were not ready. They were under armed, they were disorganised. It was not until sometime late in May that I actually met somebody who could call himself the minister of defence, and that was Mr. Doko. They were clearly unprepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, General, sir, does that mean that you are not here to testify about anything that happened before June 1992? Does that mean that your knowledge is not accurate? Well, you have testified about many events here, after all.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I am testifying about events which I knew about. There are many things that happened that I didn't know about. And I'm saying to you, in regard to this exhibit that you have here, that I was totally unfamiliar with any political negotiations which were taking place between the European Union and the political parties in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know that Jerko Doko became the defence minister in January 1991, not in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I was unaware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the leadership of the Patriotic League wanted the war against Serbs and the JNA in the summer of 1991 in order to assist the Croats by doing that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's the first time I've heard of the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you do not know that up until January of 1992, in 103 municipalities there were staffs and brigades of the Patriotic League, the Muslim illegal army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you do not know that the Muslim forces in Sarajevo were called the 1st Corps and that it consisted of three divisions, the 12th, the 14th, and the 16th?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And, General, do you know that there were some 15 brigades in the town itself, in the town of Sarajevo itself, and that they had their headquarters and their logistics bases and their artillery and tank and mortar positions, and they actually constituted more than 300 legitimate targets in the city of Sarajevo itself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I was unaware of the detail of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What time-frame are we talking about, Mr. Karadzic, in your last question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right from the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. The witness has answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But did you have any suspicions or any inkling of the fact that the Croatian side might have been misinforming you about the acts of the -- actions of the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the nature of working in the former Yugoslavia, that one was very cautious about believing anything that anybody said to you, and that you would always try and find supporting evidence for what somebody had said, and that you would rarely take on face value what was said to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is going to be the fate of this document that we have on our screens now, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll not admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to turn your attention to paragraph 95 of your amalgamated statement, which pertains to your trip to Eastern Bosnia, from Belgrade, Zagreb, and then through Bijeljina. En route from Belgrade to Zagreb, did you pass through Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I believe so, although I don't have a detailed knowledge of the geography of the area. We travelled on the most direct route from Belgrade to Sarajevo, and it was through the Bijeljina area. Whether it went through the center of the town, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. But here it says "Belgrade to Zagreb," which means that you must have taken the motorway and you did not pass through Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Then that's an error that I hadn't picked up in my statement. It should read "Belgrade to Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see what you say here regarding Bijeljina, that you saw -- perhaps we can see it on our screens, or I think all of the parties have a hard copy. So it's paragraph 95. You say that you saw some damage in Bijeljina. The suggestion in the report was that the JNA would provide perimeter security, whilst the paramilitaries would go in and commit crimes and initiate ethnic cleansing. There were also reports that the paramilitaries would commit demonstration killings and rapes; as examples, two villages: That they would meet -- [In English] "That they would meet the same fate unless they left. Arkan and his men were mentioned in some of the reports." [Interpretation] Is this, in your opinion, an accurate report? Is this something that we should really trust? Is this based on your knowledge or is this just an impression that you based on something?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: On the physical observations around Bijeljina, they came from me. I was physically there. I saw the war damage. I saw the militias controlling movement. I saw the barracks. I saw houses which had been destroyed, burnt, blown up. They're my physical observations. Now, in regard to the reports, there were a large number of reports coming into UNPROFOR in -- particularly in April of 1992 from the ECMM, from various humanitarian agencies, from journalists who were able to travel through Bosnia quite widely and successfully, from the Presidency. A broad range of reports were coming in which corroborated each other in some way or other, which said that ethnic cleansing had been taking place in Northern Bosnia. And the reports also suggested the means by which this was achieved, and this is recorded in that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know whether the ECMM had its people there? Did they have their people up there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I don't know the detailed deployment of the ECMM. They had, my understanding, people who certainly moved through that area regularly. Whether they were permanently assigned there, I don't know, but we had the benefit of daily exchange of information with the ECMM, and also formally, on a weekly basis, I would meet with their senior management for an exchange of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have any accurate official report about what had happened in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I don't keep reports, Mr. Karadzic, and I didn't raise reports. I'm simply relating my recollection of written reports which were being passed around within UNPROFOR headquarters during my time there. As I said, I had a privileged position within the headquarters that I had access to the most sensitive information. I was regularly involved in small groups that made major decisions, and I had the confidence of the force commander, so I was well informed. I'm simply reporting my recollection of the type of information that was flowing around UNPROFOR headquarters at that time in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, but if you were, indeed, kept well informed, and we will have some use for your knowledge, but from what you say in paragraph 95, I think that the only thing that we should take into account is that when you were in Bijeljina, you saw some evidence of past fighting. Is that right? All the rest is just impressions, things that you heard, but you don't have any reports to that effect and you don't have any direct knowledge of those events; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It's up to the Court, Mr. Karadzic, to take note of what they wish, but I'm simply giving you the two types of information that I'm recording. Paragraph 1 is actual physical observation. The other is a summation of my observation of information that was flowing through the headquarters. Now, I did not have a physical possession of reports, nor would I expect to have them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please look at 1D01247.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you understand that in matters of criminal law, we cannot rely on impressions, but we can only rely on very specific knowledge and evidence? Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not for the witness to answer the question. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I merely wanted to explain to the general why I am belabouring this point. I don't want him to take it amiss.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So could you please look at paragraph 3 of this document? And if there's no translation, let me just tell you that this is the Command of the 17th Corps, so this is still the JNA, and this is the daily operational report sent to the command of the 2nd Military District in Sarajevo. It's signed by General Jankovic. I think it's the 17th Corps. It's the JNA corps from Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Excuse me. We have a duplicate of 65 ter 07089. If we could call up the translation, please, Defence exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Give the number again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the entire document? Well, I would recommend that we should all look at it, but item 3, in particular, is of interest to us. It concerns the events on the 3rd of April. Do you know that Korace is a Muslim village and that they opened fire on the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No to both of those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please look at the next passage here. The commander of the Operational Group 1 -- and can we all look at the end of this passage, where it says: "One of our soldiers was killed." And then could you please look at paragraph 4, where it says, in the second sentence: "In Bijeljina, the situation is calmer a little bit, but there is general chaos, anarchy, and panic in the town." The exact number of those killed is unknown. The situation is out of control, while parties leaders are incapable of ensuring peace and preventing the anarchical behaviour of individuals and groups. Is that what it says? Is this what General Jankovic says in his report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's what the translation says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, if we go back to what you said in paragraph 95 of your statement, somebody suggested to you, through their reports, that the paramilitaries are working in collusion with the JNA, the JNA was providing security while the paramilitaries were going in to kill and rape people; is that so?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's what I've testified, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you still maintain what you said there, that your statement is reliable?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It is, but I don't think it should be applied to every situation where there was ethnic cleansing. I'm not suggesting that this happened in every village where ethnic cleansing took place. Simply, the threat and the knowledge of what had happened in the area and other places is enough to move people on. The report that I have noted in my evidence -- or the reports came from a wide variety of people, enough for me to believe it to be true, so from several different sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were any of those sources Serb?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at the next page in the English version where it says: "The leaders -- the leaders of national parties are conducting intensive preparations for new conflicts, weapons are being publicly handed out to members of the SDA in many places. At 1500 hours on the 3rd of April, weapons were handed out to SDA members near the mosque in the village of Ciljuge, the municipality of Zivinice, and the move is planned towards Bijeljina with this manpower on the 3rd and 4th of April." Did you have any knowledge of what the other parties were doing, apart from the Serbs, that is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't. I've related what I know about the activities in Northern Bosnia in my evidence. I can't add to that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we scroll down a little bit, because I would like the general to look at paragraph 9, forecasts offered by General Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So do you see here where he says: "An even more difficult situation and combat activities are to be expected in the coming period, especial until Bijeljina and along the Bosanski Brod and Derventa line. It's possible that roadblocks will be set up and that there would be provocations in the next zone."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We lost the English translation. Yes, next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, "... in the rest of the zone, including armed inter-ethnic conflicts as well as attacks on the corps units." Who was supposed to carry out this kind of combat activities in the Bijeljina-Bosanski Brod-Derventa axis, General?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Which combat activities are we talking about, please, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we see here that General Jankovic - I think he's deceased - he is making some forecasts about what he expects to happen, and he reports to his superior command that combat is expected in Bijeljina and along the Bosanski Brod-Derventa axis. So who was supposed to carry out those activities? Who was supposed to attack the units of his corps in this area, the Bosanski Brod-Derventa axis? And there were observers posted in Northern Bosnia at the time.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: There were no UN observers posted there on the 3rd of April. I can assure you of that, Mr. Karadzic. And I can't get inside the late general's head. I don't know why he would be forecasting that. And you obviously can't ask him, but I certainly can't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, there were European Community monitors there, and if I were to ask you now this: On the 3rd of March, the Croatian Army moved into Bosanski Brod to kill Serbs. On the 26th of March, it crossed and -- or, rather, on the 25th of March, it killed a father and a son also crossing the river. And on the 26th of March, it went into the village of Sijekovac, killing all the Serbs and all their cattle in the village. If I were to tell you all that, whom does General Jankovic see as the potential force that was to launch those military operations, those combat activities in that area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: You would have to ask General Jankovic, if you could. I don't know what he foresees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I tell you that they were the regular forces of Croatia and the local Muslim paramilitaries, what would you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, I have no knowledge of the events up there, other than the broad reports that there is inter-ethnic conflict going on, and the net result of all that is that large numbers of Muslim refugees are being produced. That's the substance of the evidence. The detail of what happened in a particular village, there were, I suggest, hundreds of villages at this time, Mr. Karadzic, that this sort of thing was going on around the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not only in -- just there in Northern Bosnia, but in many parts. I've given evidence that I had -- on the 4th of April, I had left Sarajevo and driven through Bosnia to Zagreb, and on the way I saw -- and on the way back I saw evidence of fighting between the communities. It was widespread. The particular paragraph you're referring to is are summation of reports I had received about ethnic cleansing in Northern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who was cleansed at that time? At that time, who was cleansed; that is to say, before April the 6th, the 10th, and so on? Who was cleansed at that time? And if I put it to you that it was only the Serbs who were cleansed and it was only the Serbs who were killed, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, I think the two conflicts are related, Mr. Karadzic. There are a lot of Serb refugees produced by the conflict in Croatia, and they had been forced into Bosnia and into Serbia. So there were Serb refugees from that conflict. There were, as I say, reports that I had received and been privy to suggesting that there was an orchestrated and deliberate campaign to clear Muslim people out of Northern Bosnia, in particular. And, of course, there's the conflict going down in Mostar at that time which was primarily between the Croats and the Muslims. This was quite a complex situation. In paragraph 95, I'm talking about a specific area and a specific time-frame, but much of that observation applies to all of Bosnia, and there's no doubt that there were some Muslim refugees produced by the conflict in Bosnia. However, it was a stated position of the Presidency leadership that their desire, and they said this during 1993, during the negotiations in Sarajevo, their desire was to see a community that was fully integrated and could live together. They never provided any evidence to me that their view was that the Serbs and the Muslims couldn't live together. The political leadership was that they wished to retain the political form of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if it is convenient, we'll have a break now for an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted, because it's about Bijeljina and refers to the same things that the general has been talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This has been already admitted through Mr. Colm -- I'm sorry, Mr. Colm Doyle.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D239, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break and resume at half past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, did you know in what suburbs and neighbourhoods of Sarajevo -- what suburbs and neighbourhoods of Sarajevo were inhabited predominantly by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I have no detailed knowledge of the ethnic distribution within Sarajevo at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you know what neighbourhoods were held by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, because I don't know all of the suburbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree, then, that it is quite difficult to say who's firing on whom if you don't know who is holding what areas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I agree it's difficult, but you can observe and you can listen. You know the general area. By the weight of fire, you can -- when you know the distribution of forces, you can determine who is making the major effort. There are a variety of ways of determining what's happening without, necessarily, close observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, but if the shells are falling on a neighbourhood, why is it then irrelevant whether this is a Serb or a Muslim neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I don't see the ethnic make-up of the neighbourhoods got terribly much to do with it. The fact is that artillery -- heavy weapons fire is being directed into an area occupied by civilians. That's the significance of it, not their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But are you trying to say that the Serbs would target Serb neighbourhoods?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I've already indicated I don't know which were Serb neighbourhoods and which were not. I am saying that the Serbs were firing heavy weapons, large quantities of it, into the urban areas of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how do you know those were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Because it was a heavy weight of fire and only the Serb forces at that time could produce that weight of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that the Muslims did not have any Howitzers in the city?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, if they had Howitzers in the city, could they not have opened such heavy fire, this kind of weight of fire, themselves?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, they did not have enough barrels or weapons, if you wish, to produce the weight of fire that I was able to observe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I can see from your statement that you toured the Serb positions. Did you tour the Muslim positions too?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure which positions we're talking about here and at what time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, right from the beginning, the front-lines in Sarajevo were set up. Did you tour those, and were you aware of where the Muslim positions were?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I did not tour the front-lines. I crossed the front-lines on occasions, but I did not tour them. And I had a general idea of where the front-lines were, and, of course, these changed from time to time depending upon the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But would you agree that it was only at Otes and at Zlatiste that the front-lines shifted and that everywhere else for the most part the front-lines remained the same?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, you'll have to repeat that question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put it to you that the front-line in the city at the beginning was 42 kilometres' long and that the Muslims extended it to 46 kilometres, so by 22 kilometres, would you agree that those lines were relatively stable?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Your mathematics is out there, I think, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Forty-six kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's an interpretation problem, not 46, but 64, 64.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's their data, the Muslim data. We can go into that tomorrow, if you wish. So they extended the front-line by 22 kilometres. If we're talking about urban warfare, would that be a relatively large expansion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: If I may return to your first question, I'm assuming you're talking about in the period May/June, which is substantially when I'm providing evidence on. No, I didn't know the length of the confrontation line. As I'd indicated to you, I had a general idea. I'm also aware that the line changed from time to time, so it is quite possible that the confrontation line got longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you cross the front-line anywhere in the city itself, in the valley?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: There were two crossing points that I was associated with. Well, three. There was a movement route to Lukavica via the airport. There was one which went past Nedzarici and Dobrinja. And there was a third one which was opened in early -- in early June. Grabaca [phoen], I think it's pronounced. Prior to that, when moving from Belgrade or Zagreb, we entered the city from somewhere near Vogosca, I think. They were the crossing points that I was familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, at those crossing points, how far apart were the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: They were very close, some less than 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know who held the positions around the hills around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It depends at what time -- time-frame we're talking about. But a general answer is the high ground was held by the Serb forces and the urban area was held by the Presidency forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I were to tell you that there were Muslim positions on one hill and Serb positions on another hill, and that that was the situation right from the start until the very end, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It depends which hills. But I've already indicated to you I don't have a detailed knowledge of where the confrontation lines were, just a broad indication, a general idea of where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the Hum Hill? There was a major TV relay station there.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I'm aware of a hill which had a large TV tower on it, but I didn't know what its name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it was held by the Muslims throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I don't know who held the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I were to tell you that the Hum Hill, its slopes go down to the Velesice area and that there were Muslim artillery weapons deployed all along that ridge, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of the geography of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say "the Serb forces around Sarajevo," what do you mean when you say that, when you say "the Serb forces"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I mean forces who identified themselves as being Serb, who were responsible to General Mladic, and who acknowledged the -- you as his political boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you make any distinction between those troops of the Republika Srpska Army and the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: There was some overlap there, I understand, Mr. Karadzic. I was never entirely convinced that the Yugoslav People's Army had totally withdrawn from the conflict in Bosnia. There's lots of evidence to suggest that the level of sophistication, the competence of the forces deployed, the ability to sustain, logistically and in every other way, quite complex operations, suggested to me that there was an organisation that was supporting the Serb forces in Bosnia. There was not simply a force which had emerged from local militias in the period March/April. It was a highly-sophisticated military machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, General, it is precisely because such facile opinions that were put forward that sanctions were imposed on Yugoslavia in late May 1992. Do you know that the Yugoslav People's Army had already withdrawn by the 20th of May, 1992, and that only those elements that had been blocked in the barracks remained?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I find it very hard to believe that any general would leave the field of battle and leave his troops behind in the barracks without leaving some elements there to be able to support them and to do something about it. I cannot believe that the leadership of the JNA would leave behind young cadets and families in the barracks while they scurried back to Serbia. It's beyond my comprehension that any general would do that to his troops. Whenever the JNA may have withdrawn their ground forces, it's my firm belief it was certainly not before all the barracks were evacuated sometime in early June; certainly not the 20th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you said yourself that the only JNA presence had been with General Boskovic, who had been in conflict with General Mladic because he had brought with him 60.000 rifles to hand over to the Muslims; is that not what you said, yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I never said that General Boskovic was --

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes. I never said that General Boskovic was the only JNA presence. He was accompanied by other JNA officers, including the commander of the JNA at one point, General Panic. I've certainly never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, they had come in from Belgrade. They had not been stationed in Sarajevo. So would you agree that the Republika Srpska Army started to exist on the 20th of May? The decision was taken on the 12th of May, but it came into existence on the 20th of May; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when did the Republika Srpska Army come into existence, then?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: General Mladic turned up in the Sarajevo area around about the 20th of May, and he claimed to be the commander of the Bosnian Serb army about that time. But I'm unaware of any declaration, signed documents, or pronouncements about armies being raised on any particular dates. I'm assuming the presence or the arrival of General Mladic in the Sarajevo area marked some sort of evidence that there was then a local Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, there are many things that you don't know, and it is clear here that the Republika Srpska Army was created pursuant to a decision taken by the Republika Srpska Assembly on the 12th of May, but the decision was to come into effect on the day when the JNA pulled out, and that is the 20th of May. So from the 1st of April until the 20th of May, do you draw a distinction between the self-organised Territorial Defence forces and the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, let us look at what we wanted to do and what you attributed to us. Can we please look at 65 ter 30655. Do you know that the conflict in Bijeljina happened on the 1st and the 2nd of April?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: You showed me an earlier document/report from the JNA general reporting on the period about the 3rd of April. That's all I know about the detail on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the conflict was initiated by the Muslim extremists by throwing hand-grenades on a Serb cafe?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that quite a few Serbs were among those killed in the incident?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look at this document. It's a conversation between Radovan Karadzic and the late Professor Koljevic on the 4th of April, 1992. General, did you know that Alija Izetbegovic declared a general mobilisation on the 4th of April, 1992? You were there at the time.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, but I couldn't put a date on such an event. But I would believe that to be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I please direct your attention to page 2 of this document. We've looked at page 1, so can we now move on to page 2? Karadzic says: "What's happened at the Presidency?" And Professor Koljevic then goes on to recount that they were demanding the mobilisation of the Territorial Defence, and, well, as you can see yourself, he says -- well, Karadzic says: "Did he give up after the Serb representatives opposed the motion?" And Koljevic said: "No, no, it's been decided." And then further down: [In English] "But I told him that this is our proof the fact that they are drawing the weapons first is no peaceful move." [No interpretation]: [In English] "Or they will stop political fights so that we can fight for peace together or we shall continue the political fight." [Interpretation] General, sir, do you see that the Serb members, Nikola Koljevic and Biljana Plavsic, opposed the proposal that the people should be mobilised, that there should be a general mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I can see what's written in this translated document. Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that you were aware of the general mobilisation. Can you see now that it was on the 4th of April?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, no, I can't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at page 1 so that the general can see the date. This is a conversation between myself and Professor Koljevic which occurred after the Presidency session, so he's telling me what happened at the Presidency session on the 4th of April. This was recorded by the Muslim police. They intercepted it. Can we please admit -- have this admitted into evidence? As an MFI, of course, like all the other intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did the general agree on anything in relation to the document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he agreed -- he said that he was aware that there was a general mobilisation. He didn't know the date, but now he knows the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D329, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, is it customary to recognise a country at the time when it declares general mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I was a soldier, not a politician or a diplomat. I can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But did you know at the time that the Serbs were in favour of a political solution and peace and that this mobilisation had been characterised as a call to war?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I didn't understand that to be the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You did not know that at the time; is that so?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: My understanding at the time, Mr. Karadzic, was that there was a vote taken, and that was against the objection and boycotted by the Serbs, as to whether Bosnia-Herzegovina should remain part of the former Yugoslavia, and that it was certainly the position of the Presidency of Bosnia that they wanted a separate state from that of the former Yugoslavia. And this was opposed by the Serbs. That's my understanding of the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we have a problem with your understanding. Did you know that we made a concession and that we recognised that there was -- that Bosnia was an independent state, and that that was, in fact, the very essence of the Lisbon Agreement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please look at 65 ter 30651, please. This is yet another conversation dated the 4th of April between Jovan Tintor and Momcilo Krajisnik. And let me give you some more information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tintor was in Vogosca. Do you know where Vogosca is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I know approximately where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's to the north of Sarajevo. You have to go across the Zuc, Mount Zuc.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I don't know Mount Zuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So: [In English] "I hear you've been informed. Rajko has told me about part -- that part. They are getting ready up there. Reportedly, they are on the move already." [Interpretation] And Krajisnik asks: [In English] "Who is on the move?" "Tintor: Well, the Muslims from Kobilja Glava."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] And then: "They are on their way towards Grbavica, toward us. Zuc, and the situation is intense. I think a conflict will break out up there." [Interpretation] Now we have to move on the next page in the English, and probably the Serbian too. In the Serbian version, it says -- it's on the first page: "It is my duty to notify you." So could you please look at what Krajisnik is saying here: [In English] "We need to try everything to calm the situation down." [Interpretation] And then he goes on to say: [In English] "That's the most important thing. Finally, the people do need to organise themselves, but in no circumstances should we look for trouble. It is very important to keep peace, you know." [Interpretation] Do you know that Serbs really wanted to have peace and that they did not favour any violent or armed solution to the situation, least of all in Sarajevo, where they faced difficulties because they inhabited only some of the neighbourhoods of the city?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to have this document admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that a part of Vogosca is inhabited by Muslims and that that's a part that the Serbs never controlled, and that included Kobilja Glava, the area from which they attacked Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender that document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, I have difficulty why this should be admitted in relation to this witness, who said anything -- who didn't say anything about this. I'll confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be allowed to say, it's very important to me to hear what the witness does not know, because there's some things he knows very well and that he can testify about very well and other things his impression, and he gained the impression that the Serbs were in favour of war and that it was the Serbs who generated the crisis in Sarajevo. And this is proof and evidence to the contrary, that that's not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness did not say a word about this intercept. You'll have an opportunity to adduce this intercept into evidence, and the witness's denial remains in the transcript. So we'll not admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 49 of your statement, you said: [In English] "Targets hit by Serb forces included most of the major buildings in the city. There did not appear to be any restraint ..." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. Now, do you mean to say that the Serbs, for no reason at all, shot at the large buildings and major buildings of Sarajevo, major buildings, important buildings in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It depends on the time-frame we're talking about, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let's start with the 5th of April, then.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: The 5th of April, I was not in Sarajevo. I was in transit to Zagreb and the UNPAs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, do you think that those buildings were not legitimate targets?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I can't comment on the 5th of April, whether they were not -- I was not in the city. I did not see the damage inflicted on that particular date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, when did you see it? When did you see what it says there in paragraph 49 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Collectively, I saw it over a period from May -- from May 13, May 14, through until about September of 1993, because I continued to visit Sarajevo after I left there on the 24th of June. I visited in various other capacities and I saw the progressive damage to the city, and I could see buildings that were quite clearly office buildings or residential buildings that over time had sustained significant damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I help you out there? You're talking about the government building at Marin Dvor; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm talking about the whole of Sarajevo that I was able to observe, and in earlier evidence I've indicated the limit of my movement around Sarajevo. But the areas that I saw progressively over time sustained significant damage from artillery fire. Some of it I physically witnessed, I was there at the time. Other damage occurred while I was not there. But by September 1993, there had been significant damage done to buildings that had no apparent military value.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what do you understand when you say "major buildings"? What does that mean to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I'm talking about a 10-, 15-storey apartment block, major commercial buildings, various other government-type buildings which are located in the centre of the city, including the library, the Presidency. A whole range of facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And which residential building can you point to and say was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, there are a number of accommodation buildings in the immediate vicinity of the PTT that were damaged. I saw them burning in mid-May, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, we're now going to take a look at document 1D1093. And while we're waiting for that to come up on our screens, let me tell you that on the 4th of April -- between the 4th of April and the 5th of April, in the morning, all the tall buildings in Sarajevo were taken over by the Green Berets, all the roofs of the higher buildings were taken over by the Green Berets, and there was shooting throughout the night, and a Serb policeman was killed - his name was Petrovic, the late Petrovic - while he was on duty at the police station. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I've already said in my evidence I left Sarajevo on the 4th of April to go to visit my military observers and the UNPAs. I was gone for several days, so, no, I was unaware of what happened in Sarajevo on the night of the 4th of April or the 5th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, General, in other situations you tell us about things you heard. Did you not hear what happened on the 4th of April in the evening in Sarajevo? Did nobody tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to tell you now so that you can see how things stood. Look at this document now, please. It's an official note and announcement of the police for the 4th of April, 1992, at around 2300 hours. It says that intensive preparations were underway by the Muslim part of the former Ministry of Internal Affairs for the blocking and overtaking of the Ministry of Internal Affairs building as well as the Krtelji landmark in which the special unit was stationed. And then a little further down, it says: "In this action, the Green Berets appropriated all the weapons and equipment and handed them out to Muslim citizens. At the same time, the Green Berets, along with the active and reserve police formations of Muslim nationality, took control of all the vital facilities in the city of Sarajevo. In the close vicinity of Marin Dvor, roughly 300 members of the Green Beret controlled that area and occasionally entered the Public Security Station," et cetera, et cetera. Now, do you think that once they had taken control of those facilities, they let go of them? Would that be military logic, if they had taken control of these facilities, not to hold on to them throughout, or is it logical that they would just leave them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Karadzic, whether they did seize the specific facilities that you've nominated or that's contained in this document here. But if you want me to comment on the sensibility of giving them up, I agree that if you're starting a war or you're involved in a war, and you seize an objective of some value, then you're not going to give it up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to tender this document into evidence now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will not admit it. The general didn't confirm anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd also note that the Prosecution was not advised that this would be used. So in future, could that be done, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the problem is that the Prosecution witnesses tend to expand on the field of their testimony, and that then requires me to come forward with new documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Anyway, General, you mentioned Dobrinja. You said that you knew about Dobrinja and what was happening there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That depends on what time-frame we're talking, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, from the 5th of April until, let's say, the 22nd of May.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm broadly aware what was happening in that area in that time-frame.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we now have 1D1100 called up on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This, once again, is an official note, and it says: "By way of operative activities, on the 22nd of May, 1992, we discovered that in Zikica Jovanovic Spanac Street, in Dobrinja," the following numbers of the street, "that large concentrations were discovered at the Green Berets, that they were located there, and that two members of the Green Berets are located on each floor in order to prevent the movement and communication between the residents, and that three or four guards were stationed in front of each entrance ..." And further down, it says: "In the aforementioned street, the Green Berets are concentrating strong forces. They're well armed with automatic rifles, machine-gun snipers, hand grenades," and so on and so forth. Now, did you know that Dobrinja was full of Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you deny it? Do you deny what it says in this document, then?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, but your question was: Was Dobrinja full of Green Berets? I would agree if you were to suggest that there were some Presidency forces in there. But whether you describe it as full, I would say, no, it's not full of Presidency forces, or Green Berets, as you call them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. So you agree that the Green Berets did seize Dobrinja and controlled it; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I don't believe they controlled it. On the 14th of May, the day after I arrived back in Sarajevo, there was a round of very heavy fighting which started then and went through until early June, and I was at that stage living in an area overlooking the Rainbow Hotel, which I believe to be Dobrinja. And I observed the fighting that was taking place in that area on the 14th, and that fighting continued through to certainly the 22nd of May, to my knowledge. And I would say that the Presidency forces did not dominate the area. That was a contested area, and there was very heavy fighting in there, all the way through to the 24th of June, when I left. The detail of what happened there after the 24th of June, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that the Serbs retained control over the airport settlement linked to Dobrinja and certain sections of Dobrinja, but that most of Dobrinja was controlled by the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I have no detailed knowledge of where the confrontation line was. I would confirm my earlier statement that Dobrinja was a disputed area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I tender this document into evidence now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D330, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you know that I always did my best to avoid any kind of dangerous situations, as far as the civilians were concerned, and any suffering on the part of the civilians in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we now have 30662 next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
