utterances.text: And do you consider that I did not invest any such effort, or, rather, did you believe that I did not do my best to save and look after the civilians? You believe the reverse? That's what I mean to ask.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I have two comments upon this. The first is that on many occasions when the issue of the conduct of the war, the treatment of civilians, et cetera, was raised with you, the way that your military forces were being employed, for example, the way the city was being shelled, your standard response was that you were either being provoked or you were doing this for the defence of the Serb people. You didn't deny the fact that these events were happening, and you didn't, on many occasions, make any effort to stop that activity. My second comment is that on a number of occasions, you were asked to use your influence to make something happen to improve the lot of civilians, and I remember a number of occasions in Geneva where you were able to turn electricity on, or water supplies on, or stop a military activity, so my answer is that from time to time you did demonstrate a willingness and a desire to look after the welfare of the civilian population of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But as a general rule, your response was that you were conducting operations for the defence of the Serb people and the creation of the Serb republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well, General. You must know this: What were the goals of the Muslim army in Sarajevo and what were the Serb goals? Or let me help you out here. Did the Serbs have any ambitions of controlling the whole of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I have no way of answering either of those questions. I have no intimate knowledge of the strategic aims of either party or the way that those aims may have been derived and agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I tell you that the Muslims did have ambitions to take the whole of Sarajevo under their control, what would you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I would say that the Serb -- the Bosnia Presidency position about the whole of Bosnia, as I expressed it, was that it ought to be one community with all ethnic communities living in harmony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I tell you, General, that it was exclusively the Muslim forces that launched offensives in Sarajevo, who then was on the defence and who then was on the attack? And if I put it to you that it was their ambition to take control of every Serb settlement, and our intentions to preserve those settlements, what would you say?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It's a very complex question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The simple question is: Who did the attacking and who defended themselves? Do you know who launched the operation in Sarajevo to begin with?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: With absolute certainty, no, I don't. But my professional opinion is that both sides were responsible for launching offensive operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, what would the purpose be of our offensive actions? Where was it that we launched an offensive action? Give me an example, if you can.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: There's two parts to that question. I have no idea why you would want to launch offensive actions. That's entirely up to the political and military leadership of the Serbs. The second part is: If I should give an example, then I would say the fighting around Grbavica in late May was certainly an example of where the Serb forces had launched an attack against the city, involved very heavy fighting over some number of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about Ilidza or what? What are you talking about? Are you talking about the hotel at Ilidza called Toplica? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about Grabaca. I think it's spelled G-R-A-B-A-C-A; something like that. It's in the vicinity of the "Marsal Tito" barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, General, who lived at Grbavica and controlled it? Is it a Serb settlement, under Serb control?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I've already indicated to you, Mr. Karadzic, I have no knowledge of the ethnic composition of the city or distribution in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you know that the Serbs controlled Grbavica from the beginning to the end?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I thought it was a disputed area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it's disputed because they were attacking us. Had they not been attacking us, it wouldn't have been disputed. You have to ask yourself who was doing the defending and who was doing the attacking at Grbavica, and throughout the war the Muslims tried to take control of Grbavica. They did their best and failed until the Dayton Accords handed it over to them. So are you aware that you cannot speak in generalised terms and say somebody attacking somebody somewhere? We have to know who's doing what and that what Mladic says and what Plavsic said, we were defending Serb settlements and Serb areas, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic put a question and not a comment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I did ask a question, here it is: Do you know where it was that we defended ourselves? If there was fighting at Grbavica, why would we have attacked ourselves at Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: My understanding, Mr. Karadzic, at that time Grbavica was important for the security of the "Marsal Tito" Barracks. My assessment at that time was that General Mladic was trying to perhaps be able to relieve the forces -- the JNA forces in the barracks without the need for negotiation, and that was a Serb assault in that area to effect that. That is my belief, and that's what I've said in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, General Mladic was in Knin, when the borders were erected and the front-lines in Sarajevo. Do you understand that the front-line in Sarajevo was set up by the local population to defend their settlements?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I'm aware of comments at the time that barricades were erected within Sarajevo by - my understanding was - the Serb people to protect themselves. That was the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the barricades in March. I'm talking about the front-line that was established on the 5th of April. Do you know that on the 5th of April, the local population established the front-line and that it had no assistance whatsoever from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I've already indicated to you, Mr. Karadzic, I wasn't there on the 5th of April, so I don't know what happened. It was not reported to me, what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when did you go back to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Without referring to my notes, I don't know exactly, but I would say about the 9th or 10th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 9th or 10th of April, when you arrived, did you find that the city was divided by the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I found that there was -- when I re-entered the city, that there was occasional rifle fire about the area. It was reported to me by my UN colleagues that there had been some fighting within the city, that there was -- or there were barricades being put up, that it was very tense. About this time, there was also the talk about the vote that was going on about the secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When was the voting, General? Why wasn't it on the 28th of April and 1st of March? I mean the 28th of February and the 1st of March. Was the referendum on the 28th of February and the 1st of March, and were the barricades erected on the 1st and 2nd of March? Now, we're talking about the beginning of the war. The war broke out on the 5th or 6th of April. Now, on the 10th of April did you come across a divided city, divided by confrontation lines; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, there are a number of questions. To the last part of your question, when I returned to the city there were some parts of the city that were affected by -- particularly affected by this erection of barricades and some talk about an ethnic division taking place. It was also very difficult at that time to -- and it was beginning to be dangerous to drive around the city. The JNA were essentially confined to their barracks. They couldn't really move out of there. They were surrounded, barricaded in. That's what I found. In regard to the -- you asked me for dates on, whether it was the 28th of February or the 1st of March, I already indicated in my evidence that we didn't physically arrive in Bosnia until the 22nd of March, that it was the 8th of March that I went to New York to receive briefings for UNPROFOR. What was happening prior to the 8th of March, I was totally focused on what was happening in the UNPAs in Croatia, and I had absolutely no knowledge of what was happening in Bosnia at that time. So I can't confirm the dates for you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, you mentioned the voting. The voting wasn't in April; it was in February. So I am interested in what you saw, not your understanding of matters. I respect those, but in criminal law they cannot be of assistance. So tell us, please, do you remember or did you know about the settlement called Pofalici? Have you heard of Pofalici?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Vaguely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that it was a predominantly Serb settlement where, on the 15th of May, the Muslims killed more than 200 Serbs before your very eyes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Karadzic, but nobody killed hundreds of people before my very eyes at any time while I was there. It may be a figure of speech, but I didn't witness that sort of behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't mean you, personally. I apologise. I meant in the eyes of the international community, in the presence of the international community which was present in Sarajevo and receiving information only from the Muslim side that was educating it and leading it astray. So a dramatic event of this kind, was it noted by the international community?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I've got no idea what the international community notes, Mr. Karadzic, then or now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you include it in any of your reports, that there was this slaughter of Serbs in Pofalici that had taken place?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: The date again, please, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 15th of May. They kept attacking them, but they finished them off on the 15th of May.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, firstly, I was unaware that that settlement was Serb, as indeed I've said several times. I don't know what the ethnic distribution was within Sarajevo and the surrounds. On the 15th of May, it was not within my mandate to be reporting on what was happening in Sarajevo. That would have been, if anybody, the force commander and the people working directly for him. My interest -- my responsibility on the 15th of May was two groups of military observers in Bihac and Mostar and those military observers who were still in the UNPAs. What was happening in Sarajevo was of intimate and personal interest to me, but not of any formal responsibility, so, no, I did not report that incident.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Do we have this document on the screen, the one I requested? I think so. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I please ask you -- well, first of all, let us look at the date. It's the 13th of April, a conversation between Radovan Karadzic and Danilo Veselinovic. Can we please look at the very end, where Veselinovic says: "We have just been running around." Let me just tell you this. Veselinovic lived in Nedzarici, a 100 per cent Serb settlement, low-rise buildings there, one, two, three stories, and it was protected by its inhabitants throughout the war, defended by them. Let us look at what Mr. Veselinovic is saying: [In English] "We have just been running around, and I shot a sniper. He started shooting at my windows." [Interpretation] There's a curse here. And you can see it goes on to say, well, I ask and what was it all about, and then he says, Well, from Vojnicko Polje, that's the high rise buildings behind that settlement. Can we please move on to the next page. They were shooting from those buildings at his windows. And then Veselinovic, the third line, goes on to say: [In English] "We now have this under control and are ready to attack that one up there to Dobrinja." [Interpretation] And here he asks if they are allowed to blow up the depot and the headquarters of the Green Beret. You can see here. Well, I don't have to read that. And then I inquire as to what is going on there in the gym, in the sports hall, and he says that the looted items are stored there, items looted from Serb apartments, and that this is where they store their ammunition and weapons. And then further down the page -- can we please scroll the English version up a little bit. I say: "It is very important that there should be no people there and that no civilians should be killed." And then we have to move on to the next page in the English language. We can see here I ask: "Who holds the airport, the army?" And he says: "The army." "And Dobrinja?" And he says: "Dobrinja has been cleansed now. Our people started from there, they are fleeing from there." So you can see that this is the situation. We can now move on to the next page in English. So did you know that on the 13th of April, there was such fierce fighting around Nedzarici, General?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I wouldn't describe the activity at that time as fierce. I would say certainly there was some shooting going on, some exchanges of fire. Until I left Sarajevo on the 30th of April, I was able to see, for 13 days, there was sporadic military activity, I would describe it as, rather than intense military activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, and if I never boasted to you that I didn't -- that I cared about civilians, does that mean that I didn't care about civilians?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I note your comment in this translated document, Dr. Karadzic, that you were asked to minimise casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see here I was asking whether the clinical centre had also been taken, and he says: "Yes"? Do you see that part?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the middle: [In English] "They do screw us around, believe or not. That is the atmosphere here. If they do not recall those snipers by tonight, if they shoot people tonight, they will kill them all, believe me." [Interpretation] And he is informing me that somehow the Muslims should withdraw the sniper shooters. Otherwise, there's going to be a conflict that will get out of control. And further down, it says: "They should be informed about it." He is asking me to inform the Muslim side in some way to stop killing the inhabitants of Nedzarici. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I've got to say, Mr. Karadzic, that sniper fire in that area was at that time was quite common. In fact, I enjoyed the benefit of a sniper used to fire into my bedroom at that time, too, so I'm fully familiar with what the situation was there and the fact that all sides were involved in sniping. This is my belief, that the person firing for my bedroom window was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You have no proof of that, General; right? That is what you think, but you have no proof?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It's coming from -- the fire was coming from an area which the local residents told me was a Serb area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now all of a sudden you do know where Serbs live; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: In that particular area, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D331, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D01270, could we have that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say, General, that they did not have any heavy weaponry, and now we are going to see what it was that happened before the 19th of April; specifically, during the night between the 18th and the 19th, and the 17th and the 18th, so that is to say those nights. This is a letter that is written by the commander of the military district, General Kukanjac, to Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. You can see that for yourself. There's no need for me to read it out. He says to him, Mr. President, your Green Berets, in the course of the night between the 17th and 18th of April, carried out an attack on the factory in Vogosca. Pretis is a military factory. It belong to the JNA; right? So you are familiar with the results of that attack. They stole over 100 Golf vehicles, and they stole some weaponry as well. And during the night between the 18th and the 19th in Konjic, they blocked everything. All telephones were cut off from military facilities. The Green Berets occupied the military equipment factory Igman, and they took everything that they needed. They never let that military industry get out of their hands ever after that. And then also it says that the fate of Major Ranko Kuljanin is unknown. It says: "Mr. President, cease all attacks on military facilities; return regular work to the factory; order the unblocking of military facilities, Ljuta and Celebic. And if you do not do this, heavy consequences will follow and you will be held responsible." Can we have the next page, please? In English, it's still fine. That will do: "Do not forget we signed the peace agreement on the 12th of April, 1992." Do you remember that Ambassador Cutileiro and Mr. Vance were in Sarajevo at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I don't remember an agreement being signed on the 12th of April. And as I indicated to you before, I had no operational responsibility for what was happening in Sarajevo prior to the 13th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But that was in the media. It was a generally-known thing. Mr. Vance was there and Ambassador Cutileiro, and a cease-fire agreement was signed on the 12th of April. And do you remember that on the 12th of April, after the cease-fire agreement was signed, the Muslim side issued an order to blockade JNA barracks and obstruct roads and seize weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I don't recall the peace agreement being signed on the 12th of April. And I can't put a specific time-frame on the blockading of the JNA, but I agree it was about that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what's written here: "Mr. President, do not forget that we have signed a cease agreement on the 12th of April, 1992, and on that very same day your directive was issued declaring war on the JNA, and, of course, against Serbs and other innocent citizens." Also it says: "Say that publicly, that you wish a war. And if you don't want a war, then deny that by doing what needs to be done." That was drastic, 4th of April mobilisation. And then between the 4th and 5th, the Green Berets took control of Sarajevo, and then there's a cease-fire on the 12th of April. And on the 12th of April, there is a directive to launch a war. Did you know about these crucial, important events, crucial for the situation in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted into evidence? The general does know that the cease-fire agreement was signed at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know the cease-fire agreement was signed on the 12th of April, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, he hasn't spoken to anything in this document that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you agree that certain military facilities were taken here and that obviously weapons had been taken out of there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I don't know that, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it will not be admitted, along the same lines --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you ever meet General Kukanjac, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 30714, can we have that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in the meantime, General, do you know that out of 13 cease-fire violations, according to UN findings, 12 were committed by the Muslim side in Sarajevo? We're talking about Sarajevo, as such.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Which 13 violations? There were thousands of violations, Mr. Karadzic. Which ones are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The first 13 cease-fire agreements that had been signed in Sarajevo. Out of 13, 12 had been violated by the Muslim side. The United Nations registered that and reported about that. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I'm unaware of such a report or, indeed, those statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to this intercept of the 23rd April. It is Radovan Karadzic and Radovan Pejic who are talking. Pejic worked for the police then. Now, I called him, and he's answering the phone, and I am asking him what the situation is like over there. And he says that it is peaceful. And I repeat that, and he says: [In English] "Except for the facts that we are in position because there are some indications that they keep getting organised down there in Grbavica." [Interpretation] Next page, please, in English. Further on, he says that there were attacks during the previous night: [In English] " We are ready so that we can defend ourselves in case they attack us again." [Interpretation] Now, Grbavica, there is fighting around Grbavica, and Karadzic says: [In English] "Ah-hah, all right. We should sign the cease-fire today, and therefore we should not -- we must not initiate any attack, and they should not do so either."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Mr. President, we are not leaving this position."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Have you suffered any damage?" [Interpretation] He said: [In English] "Yesterday, our premises -- yesterday and the day before yesterday." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. The last page now: [In English] "We have no guarantees except for people who were killed in the engagement in Ilidza." [Interpretation] General, do you see that the Serbs are defending themselves and they are bracing themselves for an attack?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I simply read this document. I have no understanding of the background to it or the circumstances, so it's just prose to me. I can't read anything into it, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is the 23rd of April. Do you know that on the 22nd of April, I made an offer to stop the conflict?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I didn't, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are referring to an intensive conflict that started on the 14th of May. Do you know, General, that it's not that that conflict came out of the blue; all of this was by way of preparation for what had happened and what you had witnessed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I can only observe what happened on the 14th of May. I was unaware at the time of the causes or the justification.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next time. We'll not admit this intercept through this witness, who confirmed nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, General, where I was on the 14th and 15th of May?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I have no idea, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you accept that I was with Ambassador Zimmerman, the US ambassador, and that he actually wrote about that in his memoirs, in his book?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: If you say so, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D57, could we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that towards the end of April, we attended negotiations in Brussels?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened in Sarajevo on the 2nd and 3rd of May?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I left Sarajevo on the 30th of April to return to Jerusalem, where my wife had been left behind in January, when I deployed to Croatia. I went back to help her pack up and return to Australia. I arrived back in Sarajevo on the 13th of May, so I have no idea what happened between the 30th of April and the 13th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Had anyone told you about Dobrovoljacka, the massacre at Dobrovoljacka Street, and the day before that the massacre of the security detail of the military hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I was aware of a firing upon the evacuation, the first JNA barracks which I think you're referring to. I was certainly briefed on that when I returned to Sarajevo on the 13th of May. I'm unaware of any security detachment at a hospital being also killed --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 2nd of May, General, the security detail of the military hospital went to the JNA centre to defend some young men. They were killed, burned, and the commander, Lazarevic, committed suicide. You didn't know about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: This is the first I've heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, obviously the Muslims were informing you and they omitted to tell you about this major crime of theirs. How is it possible that you don't know about all of this? It wasn't that there was shooting at the convoy on the 3rd of May. The column had been cut, and people were killed and taken prisoner. That was only 10 days before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, did you rise?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, a comment, not question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, make your question simple and direct. You are prone to making lengthy comments, and you formulate your question in such a lengthy way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'd like to ask the general how it is possible that he was not informed in detail about a major crime, about the killing of such a large number of soldiers, after an evacuation had been agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'd restate, Dr. Karadzic, that I was not there during these events, and that when I returned on the 13th of May, I was debriefed on what had happened and the events that flowed from that unfortunate incident. Once again, I have to restate, Dr. Karadzic, that my operational focus was not on Sarajevo or, indeed, not on most of Bosnia at that time. It was not my -- it was not my responsibility to pursue these matters. These were matters that were being specifically addressed by General MacKenzie, to a lesser extent General Morillon, and General Nambiar and Mr. Thornberry. They were the people intimately involved in this. When I was -- my first working day was the 14th of May. Virtually nobody came to work that day because the fighting that was going on in the city. It wasn't not until the 15th of May that I was actually able to get into the PTT, because I was stuck in my apartment in Dobrinja. And when the UN staff were able to return to the headquarters, they did it basically to pack up and to move to Sarajevo -- move to Belgrade. I was debriefed and I was generally aware of it, but it was not my responsibility to be intimately involved in it. And there were many other things happening at that time also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. But as a human being, you should have been aware of that. Let me ask you the following, General: Do you know what happened on the 15th of May in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I don't, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that over there, there was also a JNA column whose evacuation had been agreed upon, was totally destroyed, torched, they were fired at from surrounding skyscrapers?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I do have a recollection of that, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, since you sometimes testify about things that you did not see personally, I ask you sometimes about other things that have to do with the Serb side and you say that you weren't there and that you therefore don't know. As for Mladic's message regarding the evacuation, do you see it in a different light now, knowing that on the 2nd, 3rd, and 15th of May, although evacuations had been agreed, soldiers of the JNA had been trapped and killed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware that that happened. That was part of my briefing when I arrived back from my leave. I'm aware of that. And I thought at the time it was a senseless loss of life. It was a demonstration of the failure of all parties in the conflict, in my experience, who failed to honour agreements. There were any number of cease-fires, Mr. Karadzic, that people signed up for and agreed to and never honoured. There are many declarations of support that never materialised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, General, withdrawal had been agreed, and the army did agree, and that is what one side did. And the other side was attacked in a bloodthirsty manner. So it's not that there were mutual violations coming from both sides. What could the other side do? General MacKenzie supervised the withdrawal, and that's what was happening. Are you trying to say that the Serb side did something wrong there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I was not there at the time. I've told you that. But I can tell you this: that I was responsible for the evacuation of the next three barracks, and they were, with one exception, executed in a very professional manner, and that there was no repetition of these events partly because of the care taken by my staff and myself to make sure that there were good and solid agreements. The one incident, a barracks, the name I can't recall, became Canadian Bear Camp, was evacuated against our specific advice. Too late in the day, at twilight, they start packing up and moving. The person who was leading the convoy out on the agreed route decided that he was going to vary the route because he didn't trust the agreed plan, so he took the convoy along another route. And, of course, they bumped into a position unknown of nationality and there was an exchange of fire. There was some 30 people lost through that. You might call that the fog of war. But I have to say, Mr. Karadzic, that the UN did take great care in trying to formulate sensible plans, and that it's in my experience in the conflict that all parties violated agreements from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I please ask you to have a look at this document? This is the second directive to attack the JNA. The first one was earlier on, and this one on the 29th of April. General, this is the basis for what happened on the 2nd, 3rd, and 15th of May in Tuzla; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I've not seen this document before, and I don't -- [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you saw what happened on the basis of this document. This is the foundation for what happened, what followed. That is what happened. The 2nd and 3rd and 15th of May were inevitable, unavoidable, after this kind of document was issued; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I can't agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is an aggressive document. Does this document order an attack against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: My reading of this document, and in particular paragraph 3, says that they are to prevent unannounced movements of people leaving barracks. It doesn't say that, to attack. Military documentation is usually very specific. I can't comment on people who were trained by the JNA. But certainly in my military experience, it's quite specific, what you're authorised to do and what you're not. There are things called the rules of engagement. I don't see anything in this document that says they are to be attacked. It says they are to be prevented, and there are many ways of doing that without firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about number 4? Look at number 4, General: "Hurriedly plan and begin combat operations in the whole territory of Republic of BH and co-ordinate them with the Territorial Defence staffs of regions, district and with the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Is this not an order to attack?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It's an order for combat operations in the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not necessarily JNA convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who would be the enemy, then?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I have no idea. The drafter of this document would know that, perhaps the recipient.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you could guess too, you could venture a guess. Can we just have 1414, just one more document. Let us see what the minister of the interior, the Muslim minister of the interior, is saying to his Presidency, what they had done on the basis of this directive. This is the 6th of May, the session of the Muslim Presidency. There are some Croats and Serbs there who were not asked anything, and -- actually, what about the other document; can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D332, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is it, the 6th of May, 1992, the session of the Presidency. Can we have 271 in Serbian, and now let's see which page it is in English. It could be the next page in English. Now we have two pages in Serbian. It should have been the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have a look at this. Mr. Delimustafic. Do you know the name of Mr. Alija Delimustafic, the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us see, in relation to the previous document, what Delimustafic is saying in relation to that document: "Both we and his ministry made mistakes. Like what Bakir did or Avdo Hebib, when he ordered the war to start, people to open fire, occupy the barracks. He sent the order to all centres without my knowledge. He declared war. I told him to issue a statement to observe the proper form. He never came to see me again, he doesn't speak to me." Izetbegovic says: "Who did that?" And Delimustafic says: "Avdo Hebib." Izetbegovic: "What did he do?" Delimustafic: "He declared war on the army."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, can we know the provenance -- the source of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The distinguished Ms. Sutherland was not here, but several times we identified this same compilation of Tomo Simic, documents of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it was all right every time. The session of the 17th of June has already been admitted into evidence, and we're going to show it to the general tomorrow. This is a compilation of documents of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Tomo Simic had just collected it, compiled it, but everything is authentic. Now, let's see what else he says. Izetbegovic: "What did he do?" Delimustafic: "He declared war on the army. Four points. Signed the dispatch." Izetbegovic: "In which capacity?" Kljujic, Stjepan, realises that it is very dangerous. And he says: "We have finished the recording. Don't record this." Izetbegovic: "What does Avdo have --" Delimustafic: "Copied it and sent to all centres in the republic." Izetbegovic: "Fine, so Avdo gave support only as a technical figure." Delimustafic: "Officially. Signed it and said: kill, steal, attack barracks, item 4." And Kljujic says: "Let's not talk about that now, please. We can't deal with everything tonight," et cetera. See, general, this Muslim minister of the interior realised that war had been declared on the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I can't comment on that, Dr. Karadzic. I mean, I don't know the events of what happened in April, the detail of it. I can't sensibly comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, General, you're testifying about all sorts of other things, but do you see what the basis of it all is and how the war actually started, and who caused the war and led the war and declared the war? Do you see that from this? If you didn't know then, do you realise that now? But why didn't you know about it then?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: If you're testing my English comprehension, I can read the document, I think, successfully, but I can't comment on the background or the accuracy of what's in there, or the likelihood of it being true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be it for today, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All I want to do is test to see, General, whether you are able to testify about the things that you are testifying about.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, I can't testify about this particular aspect then, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted? It's linked to the one before, and that's the basis and groundwork for all subsequent events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are unanimous in not admitting this. We will resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 22nd day of June, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.07 p.m.,
